Soldiers' Land Settlement, $50,000,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The committee will be entitled before being asked to vote the very large sum called for by these items, to a short statement of the work of the Soldiers' Settlement Board during the past year. The board was constituted in 1917, constituted,
however, first of all, only for the purpose of assisting in the settlement of returned soldiers on Dominion lands. Certain work was done, certain entries were made, and assistance was given by the board to settlers on soldier grants or homestead lands. A year ago last December, power was taken and exercised under Order in Council, extending the work of the board to settlement on purchased lands, and enabling the board to give assistance by way of loans for improvements, stock, and equipment; a power it previously did not have. These powers so exercised as early as 1918 were confirmed by legislation of a year ago; and acting upon the Orders in Council and subsequent legislation the board has performed a very large achievement entailing a considerable financial commitment, a short record of which I think I should give.
The Soldiers' Settlement Act contemplated assistance to returned soldiers of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, of the United Kingdom, and of the United Kingdom's Allies in the great war, within certain restrictions set out in the definition. Under that legislation some fifty thousand men have applied to the Soldiers' Settlement Board, men almost wholly of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces, and the work of the board has since consisted in the reception and disposition of those applications and of assistance to the men who were deemed to be qualified to receive that assistance under the Act.
At this stage I may say that the soldiers' settlement work divides itself into three distinct branches. There is, first, the agricultural branch; secondly, the lands and loans branch; and thirdly, what is known as the home branch. I might explain that the soldiers' settlement work is conducted, under the Act, as a part of the Department of the Interior, although in practice it has been carried on as a separate institution. That is to say, it is not in practice a distinct part of the department, having been conducted rather as in the nature of a separate department, the chairman of the board reporting direct to me as minister. The Interior Department is of sufficient magnitude to engage the full attention of the deputy minister. The Agricultural Branch has to do with the acceptance of applications from soldiers; with the deliberation as to whether or not the applicants are such as should' be granted assistance; with the training of men who are found to require training; with the determination of the extent and character of stock and equipment which the men should

receive; and finally with the supervision of the farming operations of the men after they are placed on the land.
When the minister uses the word "training," is its application confined to training for farming purposes exclusively, or does it mean training in general?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The training of which I am speaking is given only for the purpose of enabling men to become farmers. Under the Act the qualification boards were first established throughout the various agricultural districts of Canada. There was a qualification board at each district office of the Soldiers' (Settlement Board, of which district offices there are altogether eighteen in Canada. These qualification boards received the 50,423 applications that came in up to March 21st last and since that time have accepted a total of 36,830 men. There have also been accepted for training 1,556 men, and the rest have been either not finally disposed of or have been rejected. The work of the boards on the whole, I think, has been carried out with tolerable satisfaction; but as time progressed it was deemed best gradually to do away with the separate institution of qualification boards and to perform the same service through the permanent offices of the department. After the men are passed as fitted to come in under the Act, their selection of land, if they desire land to be purchased, is passed upon by what are known as loan boards, who receive the appraisal of the land at the hands of specially qualified appraisal officers, and upon that appraisal, or after such further inspection as is demanded, they state whether or not, at the price the soldier is prepared to pay for the land, the board should be advised to advance assistance against that land and to what amount. Those loan boards are situate in every district office of the Settlement Board in Canada; that is to say, in eighteen offices altogether. When the loans are passed they have, in the early work of the board, been put through the hands of local solicitors in order that the board's title and security as provided by the Act should be of the character which the aid given requires: We found the operations of the board, from the legal standpoint, to be, as we thought, unnecessarily expensive following that system. No other system was possible in the early stages of the board's work because of the rapid expansion of the organization which the rush of applications demanded. But in later months we have

adopted the policy of having a legal branch in each district office of the board, and in the more important offices this policy now obtains. The consequence has been that we have been able to reduce very materially, indeed rather startlingly, the legal costs of the operations under the Act. I can give the committee in detail what has been the result of the adoption of that policy but it may come by question and answer later on.
The board has purchased lands and has also loaned for the purpose of discharging incumbrances on lands already oiwned; it has purchased stock and equipment and loaned against stock and equipment to the soldier settler and has as well loaned to the soldier settler who locates upon Dominion lands or soldier grants. The operations of the board up to the date I just gave, the 27th March, 1920, entail a financial commitment on the Dominion of $58,741,605. That sum refers to the aggregate amount of the loans approved and passed by the board, and of that total approximately $42,000,000 has been disbursed.
Since when? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Since the commencement of the board's operations.

That covers the 36,000
who have been passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That covers all of the 36,000 who have been passed and whose loans have been approved. The 36,000 men may (be said to be either on the land to-day as a result of the operations of the (board or on the "way to the land. (Some applications for loans are still under consideration, some applicants have not yet selected land that suits them, but 15,234 are actually as of that date on the land and settled there under the operations of the board.
Has the minister the figures by provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can give the committee the result of the operation of the Act by provinces. The number of settlers in Alberta is the largest. I am giving now by provinces the number of men making up the aggregate of 15,234, who are at the present day upon the land under the Act:
Alberta	 4,603
Saskatchewan	 3,117
British Columbia	 2,555
Manitoba	 2,525
Ontario	 1,109
Quebec	 362
New Brunswick	 410
Nova Scotia	 319
Prince Edward Island	 234

The amount of the commitments toy provinces is as follows:
Alberta	$17,059, 331
Saskatchewan	 12,257,766
British Columbia	 10,728,388
Manitoba	 9,789,686
Ontario	 4,778,736
Quebec	 1,573,081
New Brunswick	 1,105,325
Nova Scotia	 981,581
Prince Edward Island.. ..	585,175
In proportion to population, Prince Edward Island stands very high in the list. The number in training at the .present time is 674. Of the total number of 36,000 odd who have been accepted as qualified, I stated before that 15,234 had actually had their loans approved and they are disposed of except for subsequent supervision in so far as the board is concerned. But the further fact exists that 6,511 more have, under the Soldier Settlement Act, settled upon soldier grants. Of these only a portion have received loans. There are many who have not received loans, and placing the number who have received loans-2,564-against the total entrants on Dominion lands or soldier grants, there would remain a balance of some 3,000. The total of settlers under the Act aggregates 19,181 at the present time. Of the 15,234 who received loans, 9,981 settled on purchased land; 2,779 received advances on lands they already owned to remove encumbrances and for improvements or for stock; 2,564 received advances on Dominion lands, soldier grants.
Of the total of $58,859,069, the commitments for loans are divided as follows:
Eoans against purchased lands .. $32,173,776
To remove encumbrances	 1,834,157
For permanent improvements .. ..	6,502,435
Advances for stock and equipment 18,348,701
The board, as every one understands, advances for the purpose of the purchase of land up to 90 per cent of the purchase price after of course the valuation is approved of by the board's officers, but providing that no single advance exceeds $4,500 for that purpose. Having regard to stock and equipment, the board advances $7,500. The total advance though per capita to all who have received the benefit of the Act averages $3,700.
What are the terms of repayment?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The terms of repayment as respects land and improvement advances are repayment in twenty-five years, with interest at 5 per cent amortised. The terms of repayment of advances for stock and equipment are, I think, six years, with free interest for two years.
There is no interest charged on stock and equipment for the first two years. Under the new Act, as amended this year, we will have power to charge interest on stock and equipment for the first two years with respect to those who. have settled on improved lands.
Is all this exclusive of the work of the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. There has been a little settlement under special Act in Ontario and there have been two purchases made by British Columbia, but I do not know whether any permanent settlement has taken place in British Columbia or not. What I speak of is of course solely a Federal work.
Are those who have received aid from the province of Ontario receiving aid from this Government too?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At' Kapuskasing?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, we have nothing to do with that. I stated that fhe board advance, in respect of land security, up to $4,500, and up to ninety per cent of'the appraised value of the land. We have povrer in certain special cases defined by the Act to advance up to one hundred per cent. We have done that in a limited number of cases. I have before me the exact figures and I think I shall give those figures to the House. The number of cases in which the whole amount has been advanced aggregate 801. I desire here to express the opinion that Parliament was well advised in very strictly limiting the number of cases where the board was empowered to advance up to one hundred per cent.
May I ask what the exceptions were?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They can only be judged by the proportion of salvage cases that apply to those who got one hundred per cent, who invested nothing themselves, as against the number of salvage cases where they advanced ten per cent.
I have reference to the exceptions to the one hundred per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The salvage cases so far segregate 1.71 which is, as all will readily agree, a very small proportion. Of course in those cases it is only as respects some that there is any loss. The board is usually able to turn over the land to another soldier at what may be against the prop-

erty in the hands of the defaulting man. Now, of that 1.71 per cent-that is to say 261 cases in all-forty of those' were of the men who did not put up any advance themselves. . In other words five per cent who put up no advance have failed, but of those who did put up an advance, the proportion is only 1.71 per cent. I should say in this connection that of the salvage cases, the larger proportion are of those who settled before the Act of a year ago was passed, and before the system of qualification that now prevails was established. That is to say, when any man was ready to go and get a soldier entry, even when he had no other qualification than the fact that he was a returned man, he was entitled to soldier entry. The proportion of salvage cases among that class has been large, and has enhanced the percentage that is now disclosed as applying to the whole body of the returned men.
What I asked the minister was, where the exception was made to the one hundred per cent? .

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In practice we have applied it only to those married men who had long and successful previous farming experience in Canada-that was the definition given in the Act. To that we have restricted ourselves; and I think I might even go further than I went before and say that if we were entering upon the policy again it would be in the interest of the returned man, as well, as in the interest of the country, to insist in virtually every case upon a stake being had in the property by the returned man himself.
There are some further details in connection with loans that would be of interest. Notwithstanding the fact that twenty-five years at five per cent is allowed the men for repayment, we have already received repayment in full in no less than sixty-four cases.

May I ask in
what provinces these repayments have been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In British Columbia
six. In Alberta, twenty-five-most of them are in Alberta.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In Saskatchewan, six;
and in Manitoba, three. Alberta is distinctly in the lead.
In the determination of the qualification of applicants, eigthy-three per cent of all those who applied were found to be qualified in the year 1919. In the present year up-to-
[Mr. Meighen.l
date, that percentage has been reduced to sixty-five per cent, showing that the standard of the applicant is gradually diminishing, which of course was only to be expected. The better men-the men who had set their heart upon agricultural pursuits- were early on the ground and anxious to take advantage of the 'Act. Consequently it is only reasonable that we might now look forward to a gradual contraction of the rapidity of the financial commitment involved in the Soldier Settlement policy. We grade the men when they apply. The man who has had ten years' experience, and is otherwise qualified, is graded in Class A; the man with five years' experience, and otherwise qualified, in Class B; the man with two years' experience, and otherwise qualified, in Class C; and the man with one year's experience, and otherwise qualified, in Class D. In every case of a married man, the board insists on a signed consent by his wife that she is herself desirous of taking the responsibility that appertains^to the farm-of going upon a farm to live. Everything connected with the prospect of that man's success is canvassed, and upon all the facts taken together the board decides upon his qualification.
Mr. BELAND; The fact that a young man has been on a farm since his youth is a sufficient qualification to place him in the first class, I understand?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, provided he is not physically disabled, or has not since acquired such habits as are foreign to the industry, and that a man must not have if he is ever going to succeed upon a farm. For example, if he has become a loafer or a drunkard, then it will not do for him merely to say, " Well, I was brought up on a farm "; he must otherwise be qualified in the elements that make for success.
Is the applicant- subjected to an examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
In every case?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is not a medical examination in every case.
I mean any examination as to his ability.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, he has to apply
personally and answer a series of questions, or a written questionnaire. Then subsequently he must come in person before the qualification board. The plan that he has

in mind for farming purposes is reviewed. He is questioned as to what he intends to do, what stock he intends to get, what character of land he intends to procure, and what he expects that land to produce; in general, that man's practical knowledge of farming is thoroughly reviewed by the qualification board.
Now, in connection with the purchase of stock and equipment, and loans against stock and equipment, some interesting facts may be adduced. Before doing so, let me say that the total before mentioned gives an indication of the prices paid for land in the various provinces.
Up to the date of the calculations in this report 108 purchases had been made in Prince Edward Island involving an expenditure of $267,464. The average .size of tihe farms' purchased varied, being in Prince Edward Island 110.04 acires, in Nova iScotia 117 acres; in New Brunswick 145.04 acres; in Quebec 129 acres; in Ontario 136.03 acres; in Manitoba 169.06 acres; in Saskatchewan 185 .acres; in Alberta 187 acres; in British 'Columbia 60 acres. The average price per acre was: Prince Edward Island $22.42; Nova Scotia $21.40; New Brunswick $16.69; Quebec $24.42; Ontario $33.02; Manitoba $22.31; Saskatchewan $18; Alberta $18.13; British (Columbia $53.80
Now I will give some details of the stock and equipment purchased and the prices * laid. The money invested in implements out of loans advanced by the Government aggregates $4,777,418.77,-that, representing the value. Tiie saving to the settler by reason of the arrangements made by the Board with manufacturers has totalled $403,768.52; in other words, the settler would have had to pay that much more had he bought for cash other than through the board. The total investment in clearing and breaking land, drainage, labour, fertilizing, and crops amounts to $273,487.06. The total investment in equipment bought secondhand and not through the board is $1,319,406. The total investment in live stock i,s $5,747,108.98.
Up to the 31st of March last the board had supervised the purchase, or had purchased direct and turned oveir to the settler, 20,718 horses, which were bought at an average price per head of $151.65; it bought 20,390 cows ait an average price of $80.53; 15,671 other cattle at an average price of $43.62 ; 5,381 sheep at an average price of $12.58; 7,634 swine at an average price of $14.97; 92,723 poultry at an average price of $1.05.
Mr. 'SUTHERLAND: How was the saving of $400,000 odd affected on the purchase of implements?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the case of implements, harness, hardware, lumber, building material, fencing, household equipment, feed, fruit trees and plants, and dairy and poultry supplies, the board effected arrangements with the manufacturers whereby on the order of the board, they would deliver to any settler under the Act any of these articles at a certain specific advance on the cost of manufacture, certain defined rates being arrived at, which of course placed the articles in the hands of the settler at a very much reduced price. The percentage allowed varies in respect to the different articles. The settler places his order, ihe is charged with 'the amount, and he knows what he is getting, for he himself chooses the article. The board settles with the company at the end of each period, and ,so knows exactly what the saving is in respect to each class of article.
Does the report indicate the advance allowed to the manufacturers in each case?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the figures before me now. I gave particulars of the arrangement and the percentage charged a year ago. The percentage is very small indeed. I have not those particulars at hand, but I can readily get them.

Were the horses, cattle
and poultry purchased through agents or through officers of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Two methods are followed. The board sometimes buys itself and at other times it buys through the best experts it pan secure. If an advance in price is anticipated the policy of the board is to secure a supply so that the settlers whom the board has to take care of will not be caught at the advanced price. The board has bought large numbers of horses and cows in that way. But of course no settler has to buy from the board; he comes and makes his choice. The board sells to the settler at the price it has paid, and all it seeks is that it may come out of the transaction without loss. If, however, the settler chooses to buy for himself, he is at liberty to do so, but the board undertakes, through its field supervisors operating in every district, to see that the settler is not taken advantage of by speculators who know values better than he does. In a word, they not only pass upon the extent of equipment that the settler is to get, but
REVISED EDITION*

they pass as well on the value; they must be satisfied that he is getting value for his money. Let me emphasize this point, that in every single case the settler's will has to cover the transaction. He is driven into nothing; he decides himself both as to the land and stock. The board never exercises its activity except to reduce the extent of the purchase, but very often it does so, and almost always successfully.
Then the minister claims a saving to the settler by his purchasing through the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly in respect to implements.
I was speaking of live stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We rather think so or the settler would not buy through us; but we cannot say, because we simply sell at the price we pay.

When you
buy through experts do you add a commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think any
commission has ever been paid. There is certainly none paid in respect to land purchases.
But in regard to live stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think so. If
I am wrong I will advise the hon. gentleman later.

Does the minister know
the average age of those horses?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not; but I will
guarantee they are a lot younger than the hon. gentleman.
I hope they are younger than those purchased in Nova Scotia in 1914.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Doubtless they are, because I need scarcely intimate to hon. members that the purchase of land, and horses, and cattle in every district in Canada is, politically, a rather perilous enterprise, as well as perilous from the business standpoint. No doubt mistakes, would be made, but as respects horses and cattle at all events, the purchases have been of such a minor character that no such case as my hon. friend has referred to has come to my knowledge. The operations have now been proceeding for about fifteen months, so I do not think that any very
,
venerable horses have come into the possession of the board.
I am glad that the board has acted prudently and has not made any such purchases of horses as were made by the Department of Militia in Nova Scotia in 1914.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know about the Militia purchases, but I do know that nobody ever acted more prudently than the board has acted in this regard; and that ought to satisfy the hon. member.

A great deal of stock is sometimes lost in the West during a severe winter such as we had last year. Because of a shortage of feed, or for other reasons, a man might find himself in the spring without enough horses to go on with. I am speaking of the man who has received the maximum allowance for equipment. Is any special provision made for such cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No special provision is made; the Act does not permit any. Under the Act we cannot advance any man more than $7,500, and we never do. In the early days of the operation of the Act certain of the men in the first instance secured the whole amount, and where they encountered in the 'first year a total failure-and particularly in Alberta and Southern Saskatchewan, by reason of the drought, there necessarily have been total failures-the board has been powerless to come to their aid in the way of a further loan. The board has, however, kept as closely as possible in touch with all these men, and by means of the promotion of sales of stock and equipment which under the strained circumstances the men could do without, and the application of the proceeds to the purchase of seed or feed, it has managed to carry these men along. Even then there may be some cases of very great hardship, but we have reports from our Edmonton office, which is in the district most liable at present to cases of distress, to the effect that only a very small number indeed will not be able in some way to pull through. It would be a help to these men, of course, to extend the maximum, but no matter what the extent of the loan may be, you are bound to have still other cases for extension. On the whole, the scale of the systems that this Parliament determined upon in respect of the returned soldier farmer was a generous scale and I have not felt like recommending that in any case the maximum should be exceeded.
When I inquired whether any provision was made for the relief of these people I had in mind action taken by the department, particularly in the way of permitting a reduction of stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh yes, we do that and have done it. I have stated that there are now 674 men in actual training. Many, of course, have taken their training and are now upon the land. The course pursued is this: training centres have been established at several points in Canada: at Kenitvile, N.S., Fredericton, N.B., Lennoxville, P.Q., Elkhorn, Man., Bed Deer, and Crossfield, Alta., Agassiz and Matsqui, B.C. At these farms men who are otherwise qualified but who lack experience are first given a month's training in actual farm work. These are not experimental or fancy farms; they are simply operated in the way that the soldier is expected to operate his land after he gets it. He gets the rudiments of farm work in order that he may be of some use when hired to work on land. He is then told to go out and find a place on a farm. He is assisted to get a suitable location and he is expected to put in approximately a year's work. After that, if he so desires and if it is felt he needs it, he may get two months' special
4 pm. training in an agricultural college. For this purpose we utilize five of the provincial colleges: one at Winnipeg, the Agricultural College at Guelph, and the agricultural colleges at Saskatoon, Fort William, and Matsqui, B.C. That constitutes the entire range of training that the men secure. While they are taking this training they are entitled to assistance to enable them to conserve the money they have saved against the purchase of their land later. Single men are allowed $10 a month, with free tuition and board, and married men are' allowed $35 a month, free tuition and board, and, if they have children, $6 for one child and $5 for each subsequent child, with an aggregate maximum of $80. When the men go upon the farm, they get, of course, farm wages. At this stage single men get no further assistance, but married men are allowed $20 per month while they are working on a farm, and, if they have children, $6 for the first child, and $5 for each other child. The committee will observe that the scale of assistance is considerably lower than the scale which obtains in the case of civil reestablishment, for the very obvious reason . that men who come in under the soldiers' settlement plan are able-bodied men, and men who later get a very considerable 136J
measure of assistance from the State. The man who comes under the Department of Soldiers' Civil Be-establishment gets more because he is disabled and because he does not get special assistance after he is located in employment.
The allowance made to men who, after their training, are employed on farms, is not reduced by reason of any amount earned while so employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, they get their wages besides, the best they can secure. The country has spent $82,457.01 in respect of allowances to men in training. The estimate for next year looks forward to an expenditure of about the same amount.
Now, there is what is known as the Home Branch of the department. This branch is presided over by Mrs. Muldrew and has to do particularly with the giving of assistance to the wives of settlers. Our women officers do not undertake to visit all the wives of settlers. It is the duty of the field supervisors of the department who are attached, to each district office and who are skilled! agriculturists, to visit all the men, particularly those who graded low, in D, C, and B grades, and help them by advice and suggestion, report upon their progress and upon the condition of their stock and equipment, and make any other suggestions that will enable the board to be helpful to them. These field supervisors visit the men regularly at least once in six months. As time goes on and the success of each settler becomes assured the supervision need not be so frequent; we are already reducing these visits where we find that the men do not need such close contact on the part of the board's officers. We hope to be able to reduce this service more rapidly as time goes on. But for the present these field supervisors visit and render assistance to every man settled under the board; for the purpose not only of helping them but of protecting the board's security.
Otherwise we would not be able to follow our security and protect ourselves against men who are not making a success. These men, reporting to the various ofiSces, give an account also of the home conditions that prevail in the case of each settler. They frequently come across cases of distress, lack of knowledge of home economics and the management of a house, and in those cases they make it their business by circular and by visits from home counsellors-women under the charge of Mrs. Muldrew-to give help where it is absolutely needed by the wives of these men. They get info touch

with women's organizations in the district, Red Cross societies and patriotic organizations, and through those instrumentalities they have been able to render very material help to many a distressed wife of a settler. They also conduct training classes for these women who in the first instance are not making a success of the management of their home. In the province of Saskatchewan 250 women have taken the course in Home Economics that is provided by the Home Branch. There are 20 at present attending the school for that purpose in Prince Edward Island. We purpose doing this work in all the provinces.
I have followed the operations of the board pretty completely so far as they have proceeded. Last year in many parts of the West, and that is where the great body of our settlers are, there were areas where, owing to the accumulated blights of different kinds that all seemed to come at once, it was impossible to raise any crop at all. As a consequence, the proportion of collections was not as good as it would have been in a normal year. Last year, of course, was the first that any payments became due, and [DOT]of the money that became due, $34,307 in all, $11,911.71 was paid, and extensions were granted and rearrangements made covering $12,623. At the present time there remains only $7,693 not taken care of. It was not anticipated that we would secure in the very first year any larger proportion of our payments than we did. Indeed, if the Act were to be drawn again, I would be disipo&ed to postpone for a little longer period all payments other than interest. However, this sum has been returned and some have met with such conspicuous success that they were able to pay up in full at once. Others have paid more than they were called upon to pay. Of the number who paid up in full something over half, by reason of one accident or another, had sold their land, but at prices which fully discharged their obligation to the board. The estimate for the year to come is fixed at $50,000,000. That is less than the commitments of last year. It is, however, more than the actual money disbursed last year. We hope with this provision to settle next year between 15,000 and 16,000 persons. Furthermore, we hope to get along with $2,000,000, outside of the money we lend, it being intended to invest $48,000,000 in loans. We hope that $2,000,000 will take care of all the training undertaken by the board, take care of the staff of the board . situate in every part of Canada, take care also of the cost of supervision and the cost of the loans, because the board in. every
TMr. Meighen.]
case pay the appraisal costs and all legal costs that ordinarily are charged against a borrower. Everything but the $2,000,000 will be actually invested in returnable money, and the $2,000,000 itself is invested in advantages which the soldier receives.
The cost to the Government for soldier land settlement for the last fiscal year will amount to approximately $5,000,000. The country loses two years' interest on the stock and equipment, loses also the margin of interest between the rate at which the board loans the money and the rate the Government pays to secure it, loses also the cost of training and of administration. On the amount of money expended last year, this would mean a net unreturnable outlay of about $5,000,000. For next year it will be about the same. There is no possibility of this money being. returned to the treasury of Canada. There is, indeed, no possibility, in view of what we know of human nature and of business generally, of the Teturn of all the money that is loaned. There will undoubtedly be losses; there has been a small amount of loss already, and there will be more; but a survey of the operations of the year and an estimate of the lessons learned by the year's operations and the improvements we can make as a result, lead me to the opinion that the proportion of losses will not in the aggregate be a serious one, that it will be, at all events, very much smaller than the great advantages which the country undoubtedly will secure, not only by the increase in the production of these first essentials, but by the addition to the stable unwavering section of our population of so large a proportion of the returned men of Canada.
The Act in its first drafting, and as it stands to-day, admitted to its benefits returned soldiers in England of the army of Great Britain, as well as the army of France, of the United States, and our other Allies. We have sought first, however, to take care so far as we could of the unexpected avalanche of applications that came from our own men. The difficulty of extending the organization rapidly enough and yet at the same time maintain such a degree of efficiency that there might not be disappointment and undue delay to our own men, was such that the doors were opened very gradually and very slowly to the admission of any others. Last year, however, we established in England a board of two, whose duties were to select from applicants of the British army those who had sufficient money and sufficient stamina, so far as that could be gauged, and the right kind of experience

that would make them the best prospects at least, of success in Canada. The instructions given to that board were to exercise the greatest care and caution, to err on that side, if any, so that the doors of the system in Canada would not be flooded with those who ultimately had to be denied, because of lack of experience in this country-a primary and indispensable necessity- and perhaps turned back again to their native land. We have sought to let these men know right at their homes before they start what is required in money and experience, the type and class of man that is required, and the training that is required, for we fix a period of two years in the case of all outside inexperienced men. We sought to bring home to them all these requirements at home, so that they would not launch upon journeys and expenses that would land them nowhere in the end. There are innumerable details to which I might allude, but already I have, detained the committee and I reserve the rest for such questions as hon. members may see fit to ask.

I understood the minister
to say that the loan was on a 5 per cent basis, amortising in twenty-five years, and that 64 of the loans had already been repaid in full. I assume the department has no objection to the loan being repaid in full at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at all.

Suppose a soldier has occupied his farm,for one, two, or three years and made all the payments required by the regulations-If he wishes to sell his farm, is there any provision by which he can do so and have the purchaser assume the obligation he is under.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He can with the approval of the board. I may say that the total number of employees of the board is 1,321. Of these, 962 are males, of whom 876 are returned soldiers, or a total of 91 per cent of the male officials of the board. We have sought to confine ourselves to the utmost of our powers to returned soldiers, except in the case of appraisers. In connection with appraisers we find it impossible to follow the rules to the same extent, for reasons which are no discredit to the returned soldiers, but which are obvious. We had to get men of long experience in actual farming work, and as a general rule it was impossible to secure that class among the returned men, although we did in many instances. But apart from appraisers, 91 per cent are returned men. We have been assisted in every possible way by the Civil
Service Commission, and as time went on we were able to co-operate more efficiently and expeditiously with them. Long delays took place at first and we had to dispense rather ruthlessly with the services of many. The operations of the board have suffered at various points by reason of the inefficiency of some men secured, but by adopting a policy that perhaps appeared harsh at the time we believe we have been able to evolve an organization which is now as nearly efficient as possible. It is not 100 per cent efficient, for nothing can be that; but at least it possesses more than average efficiency as a government organization, and at the same time it is predominantly composed of the returned men themselves.

Are the valuators paid
by salary or commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are paid by salary; we pay no commissions. I can scarcely conceive of anything that would more strikingly manifest folly than to pay valuators
on a commission basis.

I have been informed that they were being paid on commission. I was told that in certain places the prices that were paid were exorbitant, and my information is that in one place the Settlement Board paid $7,000 for a farm valued at $3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman favour me with the names of the place and of the parties??
It does not happen to he in my county. I got the information from a colleague and I shall ask him to give me the particulars. He is not in the House at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A great many cases have been presented to me of just such definiteness as the one mentioned by my hon. friend.

I desire to congratulate the minister on his very clear presentment of a most remarkable achievement. One hears very often at the present time that the Union Government is reactionary and that it is working in behalf of the big interests, and so forth; but in this case at least I think that the Liberal members of this House as well as the country at large may congratulate the Government on having enacted the most advanced legislation that has ever been put on the statute hook in this country since Confederation. For the first time in the history of Canada the funds of the State have been loaned

to individuals for the development of the resources of the country. The machinery and everything in connection with this work are absolutely new. Everything had to be created to meet the new conditions, and of course under the circumstances there was no past experience that could serve as a guide. That necessarily had to be learned. While the Soldiers' Settlement Board has been operating in every province in Canada, indeed almost in every constituency, I imagine that its shortcomings and its mistakes must be very well known to the members of this House, and those who know of any mistakes should avail themselves of the present opportunity to bring them to the attention of the minister. So far as I am concerned, I am not disposed to be critical but Tather the reverse. At our convention recently we drew up a long list of suggestions, very few of which are concerned with the general principle of the work, being almost entirely devoted to matters of detail. I think that these suggestions might well go before the committee on Re-establishment which is now in session, rather than before this committee. There is one suggestion in particular, however, which I would direct to the attention of the minister,' and that is in regard to the advantage of insuring the men so that there might be no possibility of failure on their part to repay the money loaned them. The suggestion reads:
That the board insure every married settler, who borrows from the Soldiers' Settlement Board, in an amount equal to his loan and thus secure itself against loss, and, at the same time, provide the dependents of the deceased soldier with an equity for their maintenance.
This suggestion, I think, is one that should be given careful consideration, and I therefore bring it to the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The suggestion, I presume, relates to life insurance.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Representations have been made to me from other sources that it would be advantageous to have a system of life insurance established for the protection of the board, and while I have not yet discussed the subject with the board, I intend to do so.

I desire to make a few remarks on this subject, especially in view of the fact that I was very closely connected with the operation of the Soldiers' Settlement Act in the province from which I come. I was Chairman of the Qualifica-

tion Board before whom the soldiers in my part of the country came for examination in regard to tiheir fitness as settlers, and shortly after the wonk began I was made a member of the Loan Committee. I want to speak particularly in regard to the price per acre of land in the different provinces. I observed that some hon. members smiled when they heard what the price per acre was in New Brunswick, and I am inclined to think they got a wrong impression in that respect. Perhaps no ope realizes better than I that the statement is correct, because I was one of the board who decided what should be paid. I realize this probably more than anybody else because I was one of .the board who decided what farms should be bought and what we should pay for them. The soldier selected a farm and the inspector inspected it and put a valuation upon it. We did not in every case pay what the valuator said -it was worth. We even turned down a number of farms that the farm inspector said were good value at the price asked for them. That is the treason why the prices were less per acre in New Brunswick than in some other provinces. But we estimated the value of these farms on the production basis. If a farm would not produce enough to enable the settler to sustain his family and to give him a pretty fair chance of making his payments the board asked the soldier to select another farm. In -a great many oases the farms were good but were top heavy with buildings. We realized that the soldier could not make any money out oi the buildings and while they would be a good investment for the man who had the money to pay for them we did not encourage soldiers to burden themselves with such farms. We refused different farms that were top heavy with buildings. That is another reason why our price per acre is smaller than in other provinces where they purchased farms with better buildings. I know that farms were sold to private individuals, cash down for a price that we said the soldier could not pay and still I believe we were right. When* the purchase was made by a man who had the money to pay for the farm and the buildings, there is no doubt that he made a good trade but there is a great difference between a man going on a farm and going info debt for it and a man who has money to pay for it.
I had hoped that a Bill would have been brought down by the minister to extend the time for repayment of the advance on stock and equipment for a longer period. I think the period shouild be longer. Hoav-

ever, I suppose we should be grateful for small favours. I understand you extend the time for two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
IMr. OA'LDWELL: I do not think that as sufficient but .still there is nothing to prevent this House from extending the time further if it is found necessary, and I think at will be found necessary. I think the payment per year that the soldier will have to make on $2,000 worth of stock and equipment will be $380?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I think so.
Mr. CAiLDWELL:	The payment on the
farm would be $860 or $875 a year. It will be upwards of ten per cent on the whole investment of $8,000. I believe the minister said they would only advance $7,500 'although the .maximum is $8,503 iif the settler wants $1,000 more for permanent improvements.
In regard to the payment for both farm and the stock and equipment, I believe they have a pretty good plan worked out and that it is being well carried out. I do not think they could have devised a better method. I heard an hon. gentleman while the minister was speaking, say that it would be a peculiar thing if there were no graft in connection with buying so much loose stuff. I do not think there is any possibility of graft in this respect. The inspector goes out to inspect the stock and to say whether it is worth what the soldier pays for it. The cheque in payment of the purchase price is made payable directly from the board to the person that the stock is purchased from. The man who does the buying does not handle any of the money. I believe that is a wise method.
I, like the hon. member for Winnipeg ((Mr. Andrews), feel like giving the Government every credit for this Act. I believe that it is a good thing and that it serves a good purpose. I believe that it will put returned soldiers into civil life who otherwise would not be able to establish themselves under suoh favourable conditions. 1 hope the time for repayment will be extended if necessary and I feel sure it will be. The hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) made a suggestion with regard to insuring the settlers and I think that would be a wise provision. However, I do not believe that the board or the Government or the country takes any risk of losing anything by this transaction. The settler pays ten per cent of the purchase price down. He must do that. If he dies next year the Government has the property absolutely
together with the ten per cent of the price which the settler has paid down. If he makes his payment for five years he will have paid approximately one-third of the purchase price and the Government still absolutely own the property beoause the .soldier has no claim against it until it is fully paiid for. I think there is very little chance of the Government losing through this scheme but I think that as an extra safeguard and as a protection to the settler's family he should be insured. If the settler dies the board will have to take the farm over and it may not be able to realize as much at forced sale as it otherwise would. You cannot sell a property at farced sale for all it is worth. Iin that case the family might be destitute and if the Government should insure the settler it would be a protection to themselves as well as to the soldier's family.
The method of paying for the farm is the same as the method for paying for the stock and machinery. Ordinarily you cannot buy a farm or anything else without paying a commission to somebody but the Government brought in an Act which was passed by Parliament making it a criminal offence to accept a commission on any property sold to a returned soldier. That was a wise provision. We had a case in New Brunswick where a real estate man tried to sell a farm to a returned soldier. He had asked the soldier to make a deposit of $300. Our committee turned down the sale, we did not buy the farm and we had some trouble to get the money back from the real estate man. If we had not read the Act to him and shown him that it was a criminal offence it is doubtful if the man would have got his money back. I believe that the real estate men undertook to corner the farms that we offered for sale in order that they might get their commission when these farms were sold. This Act headed them off and it was very necessary to have such a protection. The tendency of the time is to make all you can out of every opportunity that presents itself, these real estate men were legitimately in the business to sell farms and while it is legitimate under ordinary circumstances to. sell real estate for .a commission I think it was a wise thing to make it an offence to collect a commission on farms sold to returned soldiers.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks on this very important matter. I am sure that every member of the House was pleased when the minister told us that in many cases the

soldier made a ten per cent deposit when his farm was purchased. I gather from that that it is partly on account of the excellent work done by the -qualification board. I believe they have been hand picked.
The explanation of that is this: the soldier farmer who managed to get through without putting down his ten per cent perhaps worked a little on the sympathies- of the qualification board, because after all we are all human,
I want to make this further remark: If I caught the minister's words aright he spoke about doing away with the qualification board. If I am wrong in that understanding I want to be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are, where we have found it possible to use the services of our own officers. We are not doing that everywhere; it all depends on circumstances. I would be compelled to mention instances to make clear what I say. We have had difficulties in connection with the working together of the board and the committe in certain points; and we have found we can work more economically through our own officers who have proven at that particular point to be thoroughly qualified as qualification men, and not have any qualification committe at all. We save a lot of expense that way, a very great deal of expense. But we never do it unless our men at that point have been tried by the test of experience and have proven true. We could not move very rapidly in that direction, but wherever we know that our men who are on our regular staff are qualified then we rely on that staff alone. It is a proper principle if we can get to it, -but- we will have to get to it slowly.

It is not my intention to debate this point with the minister, but the success that has been achieved in the past up to the present time, is, I think, greatly to the credit of the qualification board; and it may be a "penny wise and pound foolish " policy to do away with a part of the machine which has been so- very instrumental in attaining that success.
I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Caldwell) that the Act is a good one, and has worked out well; but there is an old saying that very often the man behind the gun is the best part of it, and I am of opinion that a great deal of credit is due fo the worthy chairman of the Soldiers' Settlement Board. I believe that he has slept with the Act and thereby has made its administration a success. If is not a very easy matter to hand pick men and loan .money belonging to the State, and to say to them-as an in-

dividual would in the case of an ordinary business transaction-" You must make a success of this." The common tendency in the case of a transaction such as this, where money is being borrowed -from the State, is to say: " It does not matter much whether it is a failure or not

the Government has to pay the expense."
I am very glad to know that such a large percentage of our men have made good. I would ask the minister now to give the committee this information:	What is the
number of soldier farmers who were on the land, say on the 1st November, who have wintered on that land?

The number who have
gone through the winter on the land?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean the number of men who have gone on the land up to November last?
The number of soldier farmers who went on to the land and who have wintered on the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is practically the
same as the figures I gave, 15,234 up to the 21st March. Very few have gone on since November. They start in the spring, in the month of April, and from that time until the fall they go out on the land and stay there over the winter. They do not, however, go on the land between November and March.

As the one who gave his benediction to this scheme last year, perhaps the committee will permit me a word or two in hearty appreciation of the most satisfactory and lucid statement which we have just had from the minister. As years advance on one, one naturally becomes of a more pacific and less militant type, and I find more interest in constructive politics of this kind than in the fierce clashes of party warfare. So that it is a personal pleasure to me to hear a statement from a minister who I cannot-not now- always support, in which I find everything to commend and nothing to criticise.
I am naturally, Mr. Chairman, and the committee will pardon me, if I say it, proud of the province from which I come. The figures about that province, good as I know it to be, astonish me though I do not know iwhy they should. Alberta led in recruiting in war; she leads in soldier settlement on the land in peace; and she leads in hustlers who pay the money back first. That province must, at some -time or another, have had a good education in patriotism, in agriculture, and in

hustling. The members from other provinces will pardon me for drawing attention to these facts: It is not by way of pride, but by way of trying to induce emulation in others and bringing other provinces up to the splendid position in which we find the good little province of Alberta.
The statement of the minister is a splendid advertisement of the magnificent resources of this great country. I was astounded myself to find that so many as sixty-four men had actually now paid back all they borrowed. It was rather a swift and staggering reply to some one who tauntingly said-when the minister was asked a few minutes ago how many years were to be given to the paying back- "Never." "Never," as I told a member the other day, is a long time; and it so happens that some people have already paid back all that they got. I repeat that is a splendid advertisement of this magnificent country. It is an advertisement -Which should be used in other countries of the earth to let them know what sort of a country -Canada really is.
I want to say also that the statement of the minister is a high tribute to the way in which the work of the Interior Department in its administrative capacity is carried on, and it is a tribute to the splendid qualities of the members of the Soldiers' Land Settlement Board. I have had considerable dealings-as I suppose all members of the House have had-with these gentlemen, and it is a pleasure to me to testify that they have the utmost capacity for hard work, they are extremely courteous in the reception of any suggestion, anxious to help and anxious to be helped; and they have, above all things, that enthusiasm which is always followed by hard work. And, the minister would be the first to agree with me that they have been of very great assistance to him in carrying out this Aot.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

There are just one or two points that the minister mentioned which I should like to confirm his opinion upon. The board have got the right idea when they send men to work first on a farm. The way to learn to play cricket is to play it under a man who has played cricket before and who knows the game well; and the way to learn farming is to do actual farming and actual settlement work in Western Canada. It is the way I began myself eighteen and a half years ago; and I remember the pride with which at the en.l of my first day I received
the congratulations of the somewhat waggish old lady at the head of the family with whom I was staying, when she congratulated me that I at least knew the end of a cow by which it took its hay, and the end from which the milk was got. It was with very great pride that I achieved that distinction. I have done a little better since (that time.
Another point upon which I think the minister is to be congratulated is the fact that he and the board are giving a predominant chance to the citizens of our own country. I think there is a double reason, which will occur to the members of the committee, why that should be done. In the first place, our primary duty, as every one of us will agree-it is commonplace almost to say it-is to our own citizens; but in the second place, and perhaps more important [DOT] t is along that-line that we shall achieve the greatest success, because men who know something of Canada will naturally make better Canadian farmers; although I do hope that in time with the extension oi its operations an increasing number of British and French citizens from the Old Lands will be found working under this board.
Before I sit down I should like to give two warnings which may prove useful. There will be a great temptation to take a lenient view of applications for extra loans. We all feel very favourably towards the returned soldier, and when one receives a letter from a returned soldier asking for an increase in his loan, one's heart naturally goes out to him. But I should like to advise the board to look very carefully into such applications. After all, it is no misfortune to the man himself,- and the public interest has to be guarded,- to have "to face it stiffly" in the first years of his operations. Any one who has settled on the land in the West-and I am sure those hon. gentlemen opposite to me know that it is equally true of their forefathers who first settled in Ontario-had a stiff row to hoe in the early years, and it is because they had that the sons of Canada are the men they are to-day. I would therefore advise the minister to look carefully into these applications for extra loans, and not to let his heart run away with his head-always a very dangerous proceeding in matters relating to money.
Another warning I should like to make in this regard,-and it emphasizes the warning I have just uttered,-is that the success of this board in its speed will perhaps be greater in the early years than at any other period. I think the men whom one

Mr. Chairman, I think the country is to be congratulated on the choice (of the chairman of this board; and I also think that the chairman is to be congratulated on the choice of his assistants. He has, I think, used every precaution that it was possible for him to use and still endeavour to carry out the intention of the Adt.
My experience is that there have been greater and more numerous failures among men going on farms without any knowledge of farming than among men entering any other line of business-and we all know there have been more failures in this country than in any other by reason of men taking up work that they had no knowledge of and in which they had to buy their experience. This particularly is the case in regard to farming.
I would like to give to the chairman one or two thoughts that have occurred to me in connection with this report. I am going to confine my remarks to Ontario. The

average price of land I see was $33. Unless most of these settlers Were put in the far north or in the uncultivated regions, the average price of land would denote that they had bought run-down farms. It is absolutely impossible for a man without means .to settle on such a farm and build it up inside of two or three years, and therefore he must have means enough to carry him over that period. I have no doubt- that the famis were purchased for real value, but i't would be a great mistake to purchase a farm because it is a cheap farm. It is far easier for a man to go on a farm in first-class condition, so far as buildings, fences, and fertility are concerned and make money from the start than to build up a run-down farm.
With reference to the purchase of cows, I notice that the average price paid in Ontario was $80. I am afraid that those cows could never be made to pay. In my judgment you cannot make a cow pay in Ontario at -the present time unless she yields 6,000 pounds of milk a year; and certainty such a cow cannot be bought for $80. It costs nearly as much to keep a poor cow as it does to keep the cow that is putting her feed into the pail, and this is the type of cow that is needed on the average dairy farm in this province. Of course, if a man is buying a cow for beef purposes it is not material whether she is a good milker or not; but df he is buying her for'dairy purposes, which is the principal business for which cows are kept in Ontario, then he needs a cow that will give 6,000 pounds of milk a year rather than a yield of only 3,000 or 4,000 pounds. In my section of the country for the last three years, speaking	roughly, good
registered cows have	sold at an
average price of from $120 to $180. If I were going to buy a cow to-morrow I would rather pay $200 for it than $80-that is, of course, provided I was satisfied as to the quality of the cow and her record. It is the poor cows that we are constantly turning out of our herds. Every year those who keep tab on what they are doing turn their poor cows over to the butcher, if they are straight, or sell them to their neighbours at the best price they can get for them, if' they are not straight. I repeat that the country is to be congratulated upon having at the head of this board a man who has done such admirable work and who, considering the probable applicants who might apply to go on the land for the purpose of getting the loan, has so wonderfully well protected the interests of

the country. I hope that he will continue in the same prudent, careful, cautious manner which has characterized his work in the past. If he does, I have no doubt that the scheme will be an entire success. I offer these remarks not by way of criticism, but simply because I think that the suggestions which I have made ought to be taken into consideration.

Perhaps it would not be out of place for a representative of another piovince which has received a large number of returned soldiers as settlers to say a word or two. I join most heartily with those hon. members who have extended hearty congratulations to the chairman of this board for the able and efficient manner in which this work has been conducted during the past two or three years. I would like to mention two points which, I think, have not been dealt with by hon. members who have spoken. First, with regard ito the attitude of the returned soldier .settler himself, I would not presume to speak for any other province than my own, but so far as my knowledge goes there is general satisfaction-I do not say universal satisfaction, because that would be impossible-but there is satisfaction on the part of the returned soldier, who now feels that he has a chance, and that, just as he made good overseas, it is now up to him to make good here. Generally speaking, I say, they are satisfied with their position and with the treatment accorded to them by the Government. A large number-it would be futile to make an estimate, nor is it within my province to do so-have good hope of success, and from all appearances a very large percentage of those who have settled upon the land will make good.
I wish to direct attention also to the work which has been carried on by Mrs. Muldrew, who is in charge of the home branch, and to the tact and wisdom manifested by her in soliciting and securing the co-operation of other women's organizations. The task which has been committed to Mrs. Muldrew is a difficult and. sometimes a very delicate one, but certainly it has been carried out with marked success, and as a result of wise and diplomatic management, the co-operation of individuals and organizations has been secured. On the whole, I think there is good ground for believing that this scheme will be highly successful from the standpoint not only of the country but also of the returned soldier; and that it will bring about increased production and general prosperity. If the scheme is as successful in the future as it
has been in the past, it will prove to have been the finest of its kind that has been initiated and carried out in any country affected by the war.

Together with some of
the hon. gentlemen of the Farmers' party with whom I sit this afternoon-temporarily only, I assure the minister-I congratulate the minister on his clear, lucid and interesting statement with regard to his policy and what I might call his very interesting experiment. I have 5 p.m. a few criticisms to offer on behalf of myself and others, and I make them in spite of the fact that the only criticism so far offered has been met by the minister with a reply which shows that he does not believe in the adage, " A soft answer turneth away wrath." I may also be excused, as my hon. friend (Mr. Proulx) has been, if I am somewhat indefinite in my statement. However, I conceive it to be my duty to make these few remarks and to offer a few criticisms.
To begin with, I suppose I should congratulate the chairman of the board, whose efforts have apparently met with satisfaction throughout the country. But I have this criticism to offer-and I am sure that the committee must be weary of hearing me offer this criticism in all departments -that unfortunately, so far as my knowledge goes, the chairman of this board, a board entrusted with the task of looking after returned soldiers and placing them on the land, is not himself a returned soldier. I do not need to elaborate this point; the principle that returned soldiers should be looked after by returned soldiers has been generally admitted by ministers and by members on both sides. I simply give it as my opinion that within the ranks of the Canadian Expeditionary Force it would have been quite possible to find a man as competent-though I do not doubt the high competence and managerial ability of the chairman-as the chairman himself.
Mr. NE'SBIlTT:	Possible; but do you
think it would have been probable?

Quite possible; even probable. I have heard the minister complimented on his report in that a certain number of these returned soldiers have been able to repay the money lent to them. I also congratulate the minister in that the money has been returned to him. But it would appear from the remarks made by two hon. gentlemen that these moneys were returned because the soldiers in question wrere enabled, through obtaining a

loan from the Government, to make a fortunate and lucky speculation. Now, if we are allowed to do that off the land, why should the Government not lend any of us city dwellers sufficient money to gamble on the stock exchange? We might make a fortune out of speculation and so be enabled to return the money to the Government.
You might not, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have listened to the hon. member (Mr. Power) and particularly to his quotation from the resolution passed at a Great War Veterans' Association meeting demanding reorganization of the land settlement work. If my memory serves me correctly the resolution was moved by Mr. Dace, was it not?

Mr. Dace moved one of
the clauses of it- at any rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was moved by Mr. Dace, was it not?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Shortly before it was
[DOT]moved, reorganization was already under way, and one of the first steps in that reorganization was the removal of Mr. Dace. iMr. Dace had been associated with, and I think he had been the head of, a real estate firm that had done a somewhat flourishing *business selling land to the returned men. That was in the days before the Act was passed preventing commissions. His activities were somewhat contracted when commissions were denied, but he still was in the insurance business, and being in that business and also in the soldiers' settlement organization, being a returned man, and being taken on chiefly for that reason, he managed to turn a Lot of the insurance to the firm of Dace & Company, or at least to the firm of which he was the head. Indeed, so anxious was he to do business that in some cases he placed insurance for soldiers on buildings where there were no *buildings at all. So we considered that about the first step in reorganization was to dispense with the services of Mr. Dace, and the resolution which the hon. member gives so much attention to followed very closely upon that dispensation.
An investigation, if I remember correctly, was also contemplated by the resolution. I might say that an investigation was proceeding at the time the resolution was moved, and we expect a report after no great length o.f time more fully disclosing just what activities were being carried on -activities that certainly were not in the interests of the returned soldiers, though possibly they were in the interest of Mr. Dace. I am afraid that some of the men present at that meeting whose motives were of the best, and who had no disposition to be unfair, were very much misled by speeches on the part o.f those who were most anxious to complain of a board that had not appreciated their services. Only for those speeches I do not think any such action would have been taken. I am very much of opinion that many of those present now believe that the resolution did not do very much credit to the association, and that it would have been better not to have passed it.
Referring to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Nesbitt) it is true that the average price per animal for cows purchased does seem low, but that was not the average price in Ontario, but the average for Canada, and particularly as regards the West, where largely because of the failure of crops and the lack of feed cows went down to a pretty low figure.
I understood you to say "Ontario."

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If I said "Ontario" it was a mistake. There is the further factor that included in the term "cows" are heifers, which are not properly in that category. The chairman of the board! tells me, however, that they are embraced in that designation. As to prices in Ontario the average for the week ending 31st March was $106.26.

I may say that two-year-olds' often sell at higher prices than cows somewhat older, especially when they are in calf. It depends on the breeding; and three-year-olds, I think, are certainly counted valuable cows.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly, the breeding will make up for years very often. But of the same breeding, a three-year-old is not so valuable as a four or five or six-year-old.

They do not bring the
same money, whether they are counted more valuable or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Conditions may have
changed, but that was the case some years ago. I wish to acknowledge on behalf of the ..chairman of the board, the well deserved marks of appreciation on the part of hon. members. The success of the soldiers' settlement work
and I think it has been a real success, though certainly not unqualified-is due to the chairman more than to any other man. The chairman and members of the board have all worked together well and efficiently, showing conspicuous ability and devotion to duty, which only a minister, I think, knows how fully to recognize. I ought to say here that the board has been very much assisted in various parts of Canada by hon. members of the House, and particularly by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey), who spoke just a few moments ago. At a time when the mind of the soldier in this country was so agitated that anything like satisfaction to him was utterly out of the question, that hon. gentleman in his own province, where an abnormal number of soldiers had collected, rendered very great assistance in the way of explaining to the soldiers the plans and operations of the board, and generally helping the organization of the board in serving the returned men in that province.

With reference to Mr. Dace, who as a matter of fact did move an amendment to the resolution referred to, I hardly

think it is fair for the minister to dismiss, as he has a resolution passed by a -body such as the Great War Veterans' Association at a meeting at which there were delegates from all over Canada. To say that because a man named Dace, of whose action the Government did not perhaps approve, had something to do with the consideration of a resolution passed; by this association, the resolution should not be deemed worthy of attention, is something I cannot understand. Let the minister remember that at that meeting there were representatives of some two or three thousand returned soldiers, and these men were not of such a character that they could be swayed by the speeches of one or two or three persons. As a returned soldier myself, I protest that the minister has no right to make the statement, or at least to insinuate, that because two or three men had personal grievances they were able, so to speak, to dragoon a convention such as this into accepting a resolution for which, according to the minister, they are sorry. I have been perhaps in as close touch as the minister with the returned soldiers' organization and I have not yet heard any member of that association express any sorrow in connection with the matter. The minister may probably have friend's who are more closely connected with this great body than I am and he may have heard from them, but I can assure him that I have a large number of friends in the rank and file of the association and not one of them has as yet attributed to those who had anything to do with the passing of the resolutions the motives which the minister seeks to attribute to them. I will go further. I do not know whether Comrade Drennan of British Columbia has had any trouble with the Soldiers' Settlement Board-he may have had-but he says that the Land Settlement scheme was merely a .scheme whereby the returned soldier must pay a stated amount to take up land. Comrade Mills of Winnipeg advocated a thorough investigation into the administration of the board, asserting that the local representative of the board in Winnipeg, paid by the Government, was charging irregular fees.
