I have not the pleasure of knowing the other comrades whom I have mentioned, but as regards Dr. A. Mackenzie Fortbes, of Montreal, who is well known to the majority of hon. members from Quebec, and who has a very high standing in his profession, I hardly think that even the minister himself will attribute to him any ulterior motives. Dr. Forbes made an impassioned address on the subject and concluded that the Gov-
ernment, in spite of the excellent provisions of the Land Settlement Act, had done nothing and that the soldiers had seen that they were not able to avail themselves of the provisions of the Act. The Act itself, he said, was good, but its administration had been an absolute failure. R. L. Cald-er also'' supported the plea for an investigation. This gentleman, I may say, is fairly well known in the city of Montreal. He said he had opened a special file in his office which contained nothing but tales of misery caused by the administration of the Land Settlement Act. He cited specific instances, one being that of an applicant for land who had been disqualified on the judgment of a broken-down journalist. I do not think that the minister -was -quite fair in dismissing the complaints of these men on the ground that -the mover of the resolution, or the amendment thereto, was a man who was himself dissatisfied with the administration of the board. It seems to me that these resolutions, coming from a body representative in itself, should have met with better treatment at the hands of the minister, and at the risk of having my hon. friend give me the same answer,
I will proceed to read another resolution.
I really think the minister should be asked to take these resolutions one by one and explain wihy they have not been carried, out, but since I do not intend to weairy the committee by repeating these one after the other, and since I may possibly expect from the minister some answer when I have got through the first one, perhaps I would do well to confine myself to two or three:
That all soldier settlers should be In possession of a copy of all agreements existing between the Soldiers' Settlement Board and themselves, immediately on the completion of said agreements, and that all such agreements should be completed immediately upon the transfer of title to the Soldiers' Settlement Board.
-Again :
That all applicants for loans he supplied at time of qualification with literature giving full particulars of liabilities that may he assumed and outlining the regulations of the Soldiers' Settlement Board.
Has the minister anything to s-ay with reference to thes-e resolutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I did not really intend
to cut the hon. gentleman off with a sharp or warm answer. Nor did I have any similar intention in regard to the hon. member for Quebec when he put a question a few minutes before. As to the resolutions, every hon. member of this House must have respect for the returned man though he may -

have bad faults and may have failed in other respects. Nevertheless, he is a returned man. We must have respect particularly for resolutions passed by returned men, but, resolutions are, after all, only resolutions. What counts is facts. I do not see where one can spend any time usefully in meditating upon the terms of a resolution calling for reorganization and for dispensing with the services of the board. It is only a weariness to the flesh to meditate over those things. A resolution of consequence which would appeal to a .minister would be one designating cases or phases in respect to which the board have failed.

I expected the minister to say that.
Mr. iMEIGHEN:	Certainly, you would
expect any minister to say that. That is all really that 'counts. It is not opinions that count; it is work that counts; it is deeds. I am open to receive evidence of misdeeds, but until I receive evidence of misdeeds I would not he worthy of my position or of any position at all if I made people suffer because of opinions unsupported by evidence? Where is the hon. gentleman's evidence? It must still be at the back of his head. He has not even suggested any. He said that somebody made an impassioned speech. I have no doubt that that is true and that it would have been a great pleasure to have heard these gentlemen. But what did they say; what did they And out was wrong? Where is the weakness? Show that it is a weakness. That is all I am waiting for from the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It looks suspicious.

The minister is a little
suspicious-I am glad to have that admission from him. The admission will no doubt be received with considerable pleasure by the Great War Veterans in his constituency that he is a little suspicious of the resolutions which they have passed. But the Great War Veterans' Association, suspicious though the minister is of them, must be regarded on the whole as being composed of fairly reasonable men and when they debate, as apparently they debated on this day, resolutions of this kind, they must have some facts with which to back them up. My view of the minister's duty is that he should immediately have taken cognizance of such a complaint and asked his department to investigate in so far as possible to ascertain whether there were otr were not any reasonable grounds for complaint. This resolution is only a portion of a long list of resolutions and in the long 'list of resolutions there are no doubt facts stated which would give the minister some light on the subject. Surely even though the minister does think that his department is absolutely perfect, he might have read these resolutions over. If he bad done,so he would have come to the conclusion that those who had passed these resolutions were not so full of admiration for his own virtue or that of his department as he may have imagined and that possibly there may be room for improvement. That is the spirit in which I am criticizing the minister. If there is room for improvement in his department it is demonstrated by his failure to listen and pay attention to the criticism that is made of his department. A moment ago I asked the minister what he had to say with reference to the two resolutions one of which distinctly asked for a copy of the .agreement and the other that the soldier settler should be able to obtain literature giving (full particulars of the liability which he'.assumes. That is an important point but the minister has not answered it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have answered it.
They get it in every case but of course they cannot get it immediately. They get the money because the agreement cannot be fully completed and the amount of the money inserted in it until they get all their advances. The advances are often made progressively. When the loan is closed and the transaction completed every soldier is

given a copy of his agreement and that agreement discloses to him all his liabilities to the board, the dates of maturities and all the information that we have or he requires.
How long may this progressive borrowing extend?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Until the soldier gets
the full amount of his loan.
Mr, POWER:	How many years?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would be his own
fault if it were at all long. It might run to six weeks. It may not be his fault but .it is his choice. He is waiting until he gets goods that suit him but once he gets the loan and the agreement is completed he gets ia copy of the agreement.
At what date did this system of giving the soldiers a copy of the agreement go into force?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, that has always
been in force.

Therefore there would be
no truth in the allegation contained in this particular resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think there is any allegation. The resolution simply asks that the man be given a copy of the agreement. That has probably arisen from the fact that for quite a period he is without a copy of his agreement, but that is unavoidable until the agreement is completed. That is perhaps not fully understood and therefore there is a misapprehension which has given rise to the resolution.

I remember reading in a
newspaper, some time in the course of last week, of a case where a settler in the vicinity of Quebec was called before the police magistrate for having sold some of his stock. I am not familiar with the details of the case, but the plan of the defence was that he did not know what his rights were and that he had no agreement. The case occurred within the last ten days, but unfortunately I have not the newspaper clipping before me at the present time. The matter was before the court in the jity of Quebec, and I remember that Major John Roy was prosecuting for the board. The defence was that there was no agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 1 would presume the de-ence failed.

No, I think the case was adjourned to permit of the production of further evidence on behalf of the Crown.

Some hon. MEMBERS : Carried.

No. I thought some other member might have something to say, and I did not want to take up the time of the committee for the whole afternoon. But really, sitting as I am at the present time, with members of the Progressive party, I am becoming very talkative.
You never did better.

I should think they
would ask you to move on.

There is another resolution to this effect:
That a sufficient staff of veterinary surgeons be employed by the Soldiers' Settlement Board, and that each settler, under the Soldiers' Settlement Board, be visited at least semi-annually by the representative of this veterinary staff, and all stock inspected and treatment administered, where necessary. All expenses in this connection to be borne by the Soldiers' Settlement Board.
May I ask the minister if this is the "home" treatment which we heard about a few minutes ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member read a resolution-I never heard of it before-asking us to send out a veterinary surgeon every six months.
To inspect the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member think that would be wise?

I do not know whether it would be wise or not. I am simply calling the minister's attention to the complaint of a large number of men that this is not done. I will not take it upon myself to go into each and every one of these complaints. Some of them may be purely local; some may have reference only to settlers in the Prairie Provinces and to conditions which do not exist in Quebec. I am not in a position here to judge as to these matters; I have not at my disposal the mass of evidence, or the staff at my disposal to collect all these facts, which the minister has. I am bringing this subject to the attention of the minister, and asking him if he has done anything with reference to it, or if he is willing to do anything. If he is not, let him say so, because personally it does not affect me in any way. I am not going on the land; I could not farm if I wanted to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may say that what is called for in that resolution is already the practice. The boards have discretion within the circumference of the Statute; we have no power to give them a discretion beyond the limit of the statute itself.
If the hon. member (Mr. Power) who has just spoken has run out-
Oh, no, I need a rest.

-I rise at this time to compliment the board on the chairman that they have selected. I want to make this addition to what has been said because the chairman and myself happened to be boys together in Dufferin county; and as I have known him for some years you wall realize that we are not boys any longer. The remark has been made that the chairman has not had military experience, but I can testify that he has had farming experience. He has been brought up on and has worked on a farm, and I think that experience well qualifies him for this position. In my opinion the board is extremely fortunate in having as chairman a man with the experience and ability which Mr. Black possesses. Coming as we both do from DuffeTin county-which gives three members -to this Hous-e at the present time, although of course they do not all represent that riding here-I am very glad to bear that testimony to him. I also want to compliment the board on the very efficient w.ay in whidh they are buying the equipment for the soldiers-<the harness and so on. I also wish 'to compliment them on being successful enough to get manufacturers to sell their goods at a better price than that at which I could buy them. Therefore I think we should not leave all the flowers unltil after these men are dead and /then strew them on their graves.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael'Clark) drew the attention of the minister to the necessity of acting carefully in granting increased loans. I am not



familiar with other farm lands, hut, those in Ontario are high at the present time. Some fault was found with the board at the commencement of the operations on account of their having bought poor farms, but that may have been when the man was in charge whom the hon. minister says is no longer connected with the board, and practically that trouble has been done away with. I think soldiers should be started on good quality farms. The judges to pick out these lands should be experts, because it would be unfortunate to get our returned men started on poor farms.
The hon. member from Quebec South (Mr. Power) referred to farms being bought from their owners who were retiring from farming. As far as my knowledge goes, it was not farmers who were retiring who were selling their farms, but rather farmers who were on small farms and w'ere desirous of buying larger farms, and therefore they were glad to sell their farms to the board. The reason I draw attention to the price of land, being high in Ontario, and to the subject of advancing more money for the purchase of such land, is that I believe we shall find the price of farm lands depreciate, as well as the price of stock, and the depreciation might eventually reach the point that, if the land was bought at too high a price the depreciation would eventually eat up the money the returned man had put into his farm. I agree with the member for Eed Deer that although those men may have to work as hard as our fathers did, it will give them a stiff upper lip and no doubt make better men of them.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I think we can well leave soldier settlement in the hands of the board when we have as its chairman the capable man who is now occupying that position.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that neither the minister nor the chairman of the board need any assurance from me of my interest in the work they are doing, nor of my appreciation of it. But perhaps because of that very interest and appreciation there are a few matters that I would like to ask their special consideration of. First, I am well aware from my personal contact with many of them that a number of settlers at the present time are not in a position to go on. In some cases it is true that is due to their own fault; they did not have means when they went on the land, they exhausted their loans, and the consequence is that unless they can get seed and feed, and, in some cases, even provisions for their household, they are going

to have to leave their farms for this season and make a living elsewhere. That is one matter that will require attention in the West this spring. These men in some cases are anxious to secure loans for seed from the municipalities, and generally our western municipalities are ready to make the necessary provision, but it will be understood that" if one or two men who are not suitable are among the number of men requiring assistance the municipality is not anxious to risk its money for them, and feels that the burden is on the Federal Government rather than on the local authorities.
Another matter that has in the past caused very considerable criticism throughout the West has been the tardiness with which settlement was made for stock ' and equipment purchased. I think probably that has largely been corrected, or at any rate it can be corrected by small changes in administration; but it has been quite a grievance both to the settler and to his vendor.
One other matter. I have disagreed with the chairman of the board in his choice of supervisors from amongst college men,- mainly young men. I hold the opinion very strongly that supervisors should be men of considerable age and experience, rather than very young men who have just come out of college, even though they might be able to write a better essay or pass higher in an examination on botany or some other such subject than the older practical men.
Connected with that, too, both in regard to supervisors and to inspectors of land, is what to my mind constitutes a serious weakness-that the pay is not sufficient to hold good men. I understand that the average pay of supervisors is $125 a month, and of land inspectors $150 a month. Furthermore, the latter are not engaged for the whole year, but only for the active season from probably the first of March to the first of December. For $1,300 a year you cannot get the type of man that should be employed by the board. While I mention this criticism, I would also mention this in excuse of the board, that I know they are doing their very best to keep down expenses. But since the success of this work will depend not less upon administration than upon the calibre of the men in the field, it is a poor point at which to attempt economies; and I think that you need rather to employ inspectors the year round at good salaries, and to employ supervisors who have had some experience and

who can command better pay because they can give better service.

I rise to make one observation in regard to this matter. Before doing so I wish to endorse what the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis) has said in respect to supervisors. I think the board would be well advised to employ older men, for although these young fellows coming out of college may have the technical education, they have not the practical experience.
When the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) rose to speak this afternoon he drew attention to the fact that he was speaking from this particular end of the Chamber, and he hastened to inform the committee that he was only here for the time being. Now, Sir, I believe if the member for Quebec South were to decide to sit with this group permanently it might be necessary for him to revise his views in some particulars. It is only a few weeks ago that the hon. member in a very able address charged the Agrarians or the farmers of this country with profiteering-at least, he tried to put them in the profiteer class. That is one thing he would have to disabuse his mind of.
When I returned to the West last fall I took occasion to meet the returned men in my constituency at a number of places, and their big criticism was the slowness with which inspections were made in Saskatchewan last year. I was informed by returned men that in some cases options that had been taken upon land expired befoie inspection and valuation was made. Again, in many cases inspection had not been made before the snow was on the ground, and during the winter the men were in a state of uncertainty as to whether or not they were going to get the lands. I hope the minister will see to it that this year the inspections are cleaned up early in the fall so that the men will not be kept in suspense.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I wish to refer to some remarks made by the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis), supplemented and supported by my hon. friend (Mr. Johnston). The criticism was that there should not be such an adherence to young men, particularly agricultural college graduates, in the selection of supervisors. The duty of the field supervisor is to visit and assist the settler periodically after he goes on the land. There would be advantage in securing older men-experienced, successful farmers-but 1371
the difficulties are twofold. First, experienced, successful farmers are not available in these times at the prices which the board are able to pay. The conditions under which farming has been carried on during the last eight years have been too favourable to make it pay for a farmer to take a position of this kind for only part of the year at $150 a month. But secondly, and more important, we have been anxious to the utmost of our ability to secure returned men. Now, we cannot as a rule take returned men as appraisers, for the reasons that I have given; consequently we are more than anxious to take them as field supervisors, and we do so take them. It is very hard to get a returned man who is anything but a fairly young man and who at the same time knows agriculture. If you are going to have a returned man, and also an agriculturist, then about the best you can select is the agricultural college graduate who is a returned man. Consequently, our field supervisors are predominatingly of that class.
The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) states that he has heard of cases of delay in Saskatchewan in the securing of valuations. There undoubtedly has been delay in winter. We have consistently refused to inspect land when it is under snow; I do not feel that we can do it when the land is under snow, and do it right. Consequently there is delay then, but the settler will simply have to put up with it because we cannot have winter inspections and at the same time protect the interests of the board. I do not think that there has been any general delay in summer. There [DOT]may have been a few individual cases, but none of them have come to my ears until now, and the settlers are not slow to write me if there is anything wrong. The average time between application and the completion of inspection is between two and three weeks, and that is certainly not long. There were inspected in Saskatchewan last year approximately 5,600 farms, so that with the limited staff at our disposal the hon. member will see that there has been anything but lethargy in the carrying on of the work.

I have passed this information on to the minister as it came to me, but I wish to impress upon the minister that it is imperative that the inspection be cleaned up in the fall so that the mqn will not have to be in uncertainty during the winter months. As to the employment of returned men, my view is that returned

man should he employed where-
6 p.m. ever possible, other things being equal. But I would not employ a returned man if I thought I could get a better man. I would say that in respect to the chairman of this board; I believe that he is the right man for the position, and from the fact that he is the right man there results a benefit to all returned men.

In New Brunswick we were able to keep up with the inspection branch of the work all right, but. our trouble was to get the legal documents uade out after the purchase had been made. As a member of the local branch in our province I know that recommendations were made time and again to the chairman of the board that a solicitor should be provided for each county to look up the records and get out the papers without delay after a purchase was made. In a number of cases last summer we had so much delay that we had to get authority to make agreements of sale between the board and the man frota whom we were buying, pending the making out of the formal legal documents, and in that way we got the settlers on the land in time to harvest the crops; otherwise, that would have been impossible. In fact, those from whom the lands are purchased do not want to wait three months before the transfir is effected and the money is paid, and they do not feel like giving up the farm to ?he settler until they have something more reliable than a man's word for it that the price stated will be paid for the property. Our solicitor in New Brunswick had quite a large practice of his own, and he said that he simply did not have time to keep up with all the word. This soldier settlement work had to wait until he got his own work done,-that is, if he did not farm it out to some one else. In that respect I think some improvement might be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If we had a solicitor in each county the cost would be utterly indefensible, if not startling. By our system of having a solicitor in the service of the board-I think that is the case in New Brunswick-we get more expeditious results, and we have reduced the legal costs allowed to lawyers in respect of searching titles for the board from an average of $20 to $22 per title to about $4 per title. In Alberta alone we saved by that method $180,000 in eight months. We are extending the system throughout the whole Dominion.

My proposal would
not be to employ a solicitor in each county

to devote his whole time to the work. In our province we had offers from solicitors in the different counties to take up this work at so much per deed, and I believe that the work could have been done just as cheaply in New Brunswick if we had so employed a man in each county. Several lawyers from different counties talked to me about this .matter. I am not sure that you could get- it done for $4 each. That looks to me very cheap, because my experience with lawyers has been that they will hardly bid you the time of day for less than that.

["I wish I could in the brevity of my remarks make them as pithy in one direction as I am sure the Chairman of the Committee would wish; but there are limitations of course which we find ourselves in contact with, and which, whether we wish it or not, restrain in many ways the practical embodiment of the sympathies and goodwill of the Government.
I have been particularly pleased with the tone of the debate-not speaking of tone in the usual way, but in regard to the line of intelligent appreciation and presentation of the subject itself. Not merely a sentimental support has been given, but a support of insight and of real connection between the mind and the heart of the speaker and the principles of the subject under discussion.
As one heard successive speakers talking of the marvellous things which had been done by science, and which we ourselves had forgotten in a good many respects until they were brought to our attention to-night, one wondered why people run into other channels for the wonders of romance. Really

the greatest romances, particularly of the last centuries, have been found in the development of scientific thought and in the scientific research earned on by the quiet workers of the world. They come upon us one after the other; the story passes, and then we are apt to forget. When we have a summing up, such as we have had to-night, we are impressed with the wonderful phases of the development of humanity which has taken place during the last fifty, sixty or one hundred years.
As to the matter which is directly before us, I will spare the blushes of the member for London (Mr. Cronyn) by not reiterating what has already been said by many of those who have spoken. But while sparing his blushes, I do not want him to think that I do not in my heart thank him for the work which he and his willing and efficient committee have performed in connection with this matter and for the way in which they have presented the subject to us to-night. We must not forget, either, that during the l^st five years, as was mentioned by the member for Calgary West (Mr. Tweedie) we have been doing a little towards maintaining and extending the interest in this matter through the Advisory Research Council. Things of this kind proceed step by step,- here a little, and there a little. Without a doubt we are working up to the point where we shall have in Canada some such efficient mechanism as has been described here to-night. I wish we could work it out now, but there are considerations which make that difficult. I am not, however, without hope that we may, even this year, -make a beginning in the direction of carrying out the report-something, at least, which will be an earnest of the completion of the project as soon as possible. In a way, it is a kind of irony that the very thing which has made it particularly necessary that an impetus should be given to scientific research and the alliance of scientific effort with industrial development, the war, has so crippled us that we cannot do what we would like to do in this respect. Science does two things: it puts within the power of the destructive elements of war vast enginery and machinery for completing the destruction upon which it is bent, and almost at the same time it stretches out the hand of solace, comfort, help to the victims of the destruction which it has thus helped to create. If the war has made wounds, deep and gaping, and broad, and if science has helped to make those wounds, science to-day is putting all its resources and its effort into the healing of those wounds, into the
bringing of a normal period and, subsequently, a more progressive period of development in all these matters, not leaving out that which is probably the greatest good that can come from the development of science,-the betterment of the world and the greater wellbeing of all those who live in it. For after all, science is to he judged, not by the material development which it first brings about, but by the extent to which it promotes the comfort, happiness and uplift of the people; by the general good which it accomplishes for the world.
I want to reiterate my thanks and the thanks of the Government for the good work which hals been done by the member for London and his committee, and to assure them that it will not be allowed to pass without fruit. I hope that something may be done alt an early day; that if all we would like - to do cannot be 'accomplished, at least a beginning may be made. I shall bring the matter to the- attention of my colleagues, and I know that I shall have a sympathetic set of colleagues, whether or not we 'shall be table to cross all the ditches and make all the progress we would like to make at this particular time."]

When the committee
rose at six o-'clo-ck we had, I 'believe, just terminated the discussion on this item. Shall the item carry?

Before the item carries,
Mr. Chairman; I have a large number of resolutions, passed by the Great War Veterans in convention assembled, to bring to the attention of the minister. Some of these resolutions have already been- discuss^ ed, but I am under the impression that owing to the fact that very important business is to come on later time will perhaps be saved were I to ask the minister to obtain through his very efficient department, copies of these resolutions and see to it that they are placed before the committee now sitting on Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. This committee, I am sure, will be in a position to deal with matters affecting the-re-establishment of the soldier, as it has already dealt with the question of pensions. But before asking the minister to do this, I would like to draw his attention particularly to some of the resolutions in the hope that he will be able to settle the grievances complained of, and thus relieve the committee referred to of the necessity of bringing in any recommendations.
One of the resolutions asks that the Settlement Board make arrangements for the breaking of wild lands in any locality where there are large soldier settlements; and another recommends that all leased lands be re-inspected and re-classified immediately, and that such inspection be conducted by experts other than branch inspectors. There are a number of others with reference to w'aste land; and one in particular with reference to Dominion lands which recommends that- service in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces be held equivalent to residence and duty done irrespective of w'het-her the entry was made prior or subsequent to enlistment. As I said before, it may not, perhaps, serve any useful purpose to take up the time of the House with this matter, but there is no doubt that the soldiers appear to have a real grievance, and this grievance should receive a hearing from some authority. The best possible body at present constituted for that purpose is the Committee of Reestablishment.
Before closing, however, I would like to make this statement,

that though it is rather early to unduly criticize the whole policy of re-establishment, it does seem to me that if this is intended to be a policy of colonization, in the old provinces at any rate, it has failed of its purpose, inasmuch as old farms are being taken up by new settlers who may or may not make agricultural experts, and so for the time -during which greater production is needed that

greater production will not be obtained. If this scheme is intended for re-establishment of our soldiers, it sins in this respect, that we are re-establishing one class of soldiers at the expense of all the other classes. On the principle of giving equal justipe to all the Government should make some provision whereby other soldiers will also be enabled to re-establish themselves.

Mr. Chairman, when we take into account the magnitude of this undertaking, the very large amount of money involved, and the great number of soldiers to be dealt with, and, further, when we consider that the whole matter is new and that the minister and his associates have had nothing to guide them in working out this intricate problem, it appears to me that he and the board of management are entitled to the greatest possible commendation.
Prom every point of view the report presented to this committee is admirable. I can scarcely permit the occasion to pass without making a brief reference to the province from which I come-Prince Edward Island, and to express my gratification at the excellent showing that this small province-'the smallest in Confederation - has made. According to the report 234 settlements were made, which is a very large number in proportion to the total population of the province. Not only that, Mr. Chairman, but the high average value per acre of the lands appropriated for settlement in that province, over $22 is most gratifying, it being the third highest, British Columbia coming first and Alberta second. Another very agreeable fact is that among these 234 soldiers who were settled on the Island only one failed to make good, which is a very pleasant feature indeed.
On the whole, then, when we consider this question in all its phases,-the enormous amount of money involved and the magnitude of the work-and when we contrast the intricacy of the problems to be solved with the marked success that has attended the solution of those problems by the minister and his board of management, and especially by the chairman of that board, I say again, Mr. Chairman, that all concerned are deserving of the highest praise.

I want to take this opportunity of putting in a good word for the chairman of the Soldiers' Settlement Board, Doctor Black. I have had a good deal of correspondence with him and numerous conversations, and I know him to be perfectly efficient, and that his heart is in the work. Why he was appointed rather than a re-

turned soldier I cannot say, but possibly at the time there was no sufficiently qualified' returned soldier available. I can say, however, from my experience of Dr. Black that he was a good choice; he is doing his work well and, I think, in the interests of the soldiers. I understand that about 90 per cent of the officials of the board are returned soldiers, which is a very fair showing.
There have been, however, some defects in local administration. I take a good deal of interest in the work of the board, and last fall I spent several weeks in ordeT to ascertain how the Soldiers' Settlement Act was working out in practice. I found very few complaints of wrong valuations (there were some, of course); but there weTe numerous complaints of delays in land valuation and stock inspection. Delays in land valuation have already been dealt with this afternoon, and I need only add that I know of cases where the applications were approved in the middle of the summer or even earlier, but inspections were not made, and, of course, when the snow came those inspections were hung up until the following spring. Now, it seems to me that in many cases this delay was entirely inexcusable. A few weeks should be all that is necessary between the time of the application being approved and the inspection being made. Those soldiers whose inspections were delayed have had to wait until spring, not only for the valuation of the land, but if that is approved, for the valuation of the stock, and that means that they are losing a year. I am speaking, of course, of men who want to buy improved farms.
There are two classes of inspection: Land valuating, and stock and implement inspection. A good land man may not be a good stock man; and the converse may be the case. I think, though, that wherever possible the duties should be combined, and that when a man makes a valuation of the land, if he is a capable man, he should also make an inspection of the stock and implements. But in any event, there is no reason why stock and implement inspection should be delayed on account of the snow. I found a large number of men whose land had been inspected did not know what to do-they were losing options in stock ,and good markets, and weTe very much discontented. I took the matter up at Regina, and a very good land valuator was authorized, who, however, at that time had no authority to inspect stock and implements, although he was a first-class man at this work. He was called into Regina and given instructions to go over the district I

am speaking about-my own constituency- and as I kept in touch with him and also with the returned men by phone and otherwise, I found that he was doing good work. He had had sixty or seventy cases to start with. The men were waiting for an inspection which could have been made considerably earlier. However, most of these oases have been dealt with, and there has been a great improvement along this line which I hope will continue. This plan for the settlement of soldiers upon the land is a good one if you get the right men on the right kind of land and deal with them in a proper way. But you must give them a good start; if they get a bad start it will be hard for them to make up. They have a good deal on their shoulders, but after all they are called upon to pay an interest rate of only a little more than seven per cent on the cost of the land which covers principal as well. If a man went to a loan company he would probably have to pay eight per cent or thereabouts simply for the use of the money. I do think, however, that in the matter of repayment, the amounts allowed for stock and implements should, if possible, be put on the same basis as amounts allowed for land. Of course, the amount is amortized for four years, the first two years without interest. But even so, the first few years are going to be most difficult for the settler. I know that the whole thing has to be done on business lines, but in any case the land is responsible for the whole debt incurred by the settler when he takes advantage of this loan together with the stock and implements. Moreover, the land would increase in value as time went on, and the Government would still have good security. The suggestion that the amounts which are expended u,pon the purchase of stock and implements should be included with the land payments is one which I think is well worthy of consideration, in the general interests of soldier settlement. As to the defects of local administration to which I have referred, I believe that the machinery is now runing more smoothly under the chairmanship of iDt. (Black, who has kept in touch with matters of this kind, and I am satisfied that the plan will work well in the future.
Mr. MORPHY': So many uniformly delightful things have been said to-day about the administration of this department that a changed condition has been brought about in this Chamber. It is rather pleasing to me, as one who has had a good deal to do with individual cases before the
Soldiers' Settlement Board, to find that my experience has been the general experience of all those who have spoken and who have had dealings with the board. It is true that the encomiums have come largely from friends of the third or Agrarian party, and from this side of the House. Whether it is because these hon. gentlemen have taken a keener interest in the welfare of the soldier than hon. gentlemen opposite, I do not know; but it struck me as rather peculiar that all the commendatory remarks had come from these two sides of the House. They have come, I believe, from the sincerity of the hearts of those who have had to do with the board. My mind reverts to the time when this board was being formed. All kinds of predictions of disaster were made; the Government were entering it was said, upon a ruinous undertaking the end of which no man knew. The country would be impoverished; the soldier would fall down in the undertaking and leave his debts unpaid; there would be a great financial loss all round. It is rather pleasing to know now from the minister that the scheme has been well thought out and that to-day we have fifteen or sixteen thousand returned soldiers on the land, practically all making good-so good that already some of them have been able to pay back to the Government, long before the repayment was required, the money that was advanced to them. This is a hopeful sign, because it will operate as an incentive to those who have yet to take up land under the soldier settlement scheme. So that we have launched upon the sea of Canadian life a scheme which goes to re-establish the soldier, to put him upon his feet, to enable him to make a first-class living for himself, and which also ensures to the consumers of the country a vastly greater production than would have been the case had this plan not been adopted. In this early period of reconstruction it is pleasing to find this branch of soldier settlement and reestablishment meeting with a great measure of success. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) who would have had to take the responsibility for failure, is entitled to the credit for the success of the scheme, and so far as it has been a success I join with other hon. gentlemen who have congratulated him. But the thing that struck me more than anything else in my dealing with the board was the manner in which the service outside of Ottawa- in Toronto, for instance-was carried on. A great deal of credit is due to Dr. Black

for having followed the example of the minister in getting round him a good staff and in prosecuting the work outside of what we might call headquarters. The executive in Toronto are up-to-date, businesslike, prompt, courteous, and altogether alive to the work that they have to do. I congratulate Dr. Black on his services and on the services of those whom he has seen fit to bring into the country's service under him. I have great pleasure in giving this testimony, based, as it is, upon my own personal experience.
