I beg to move:
That the first report of the Special Committee appointed to enquire into the matter of the development in Canada of scientific research be now considered and that the recommendations thereof be commended to the consideration of the Government.
It is not uncommon when a member of the House rises to introduce a resolution of this type to hear him state that the matter is one of prime importance, nor is it hard to understand such a declaration, because if the matter at issue did not in the mind of the mover seem to be important he doubtless would have hesitated to bring it to the attention of the House. When, therefore, by way of introduction, I assert my belief that the resolution and the report it seeks to confirm are of importance to the country, I am but affirming my pronounced conviction on that point. Doubtless matters already debated in the House, and to be debated, are rightly classed as important, but I doubt if there be one whose influence, if carried to conclusion, would be as widespread and enduring, at least to the material prosperity of Canada, as ..that dealing with scientific industrial

research. I therefore crave a hearing and consideration from the members to the remarks that may follow in this debate, as I am above all anxious that Parliament and the country shall understand the recommendations of the committee. My part of the task will be to co-ordinate the report made at the spring session of last year with the present report, as the latter is the logical outcome of what previously occurred.
Let me go back for a moment to review what has happened. Some three years ago under the terms of an Act passed by this Parliament an Honourary Advisory Council was appointed to survey the present situation in this respect and to report thereon. After very carefully considering the matter and making numerous and widespread inquiries, consulting those both here and abroad best fitted to express an opinion, the council reached the conclusion that scientific industrial research was worthy of support by this Dominion, and that such support could most effectively be applied by the foundation of a central research institute in or near the capital of the country. For more extended reference to these reports I would direct the House to the reports of the administrative chairman of the council which have from time to time been laid on the Table. During the spring session of last year a Select Parliamentary Committee was appointed to inquire into the whole matter and I would ask leave to read one or two extracts from their report:
Upon consideration of the whole question, your committee beg to report that scientific research in Canada requires and deserves generous encouragement and financial support from the Dominion Government. In no better way can the natural resources of our country be made available with the same degree of celerity and certainty, nor can our native industries achieve their proper position in the markets of the world unless given the advantages accruing from scientific research and discovery.
Your committee feel that the time has arrived when further steps must be taken and additional financial support be available if this country desires to make a proper use of its potential assets and to attain or maintain its standing in the commonwealth of nations.
The attention of your committee has been directed to the fact that there does not exist in this country any institution corresponding to the Bureau of Standards at "Washington. As a result, Canada is dependent on the neighbouring republic or on other countries for information and guidance in matters which vitally concern her industries. A study of the evidence submitted will convince any impartial student of the weakness of our position in this regard and of the need for a speedy remedy. Your committee, therefore, recommend to the consid-

eration of the Government the establishment of a Dominion Bureau of Standards.
While your committee, as above stated, are unanimous as to the need of co-operation and national support of scientific research, yet a majority of its members, owing to the lack of time and pressure of other parliamentary duties, feel they have been unable to so consider and digest the evidence adduced and the other material brought to their attention as to advise the House at this time what may be the best method of aiding and encouraging scientific research throughout Canada.
These extracts are from the report-of the committee of a year ago. The committee appointed this session has given consideration to the question raised by the former committee, and the report iwhich has just been tabled shows the findings of the committee in that respect. As, possibly, that report has not been read by most of the members present I might make a short review of its contents.
After reciting the situation in somewhat the same language that I have just used the report goes on record ais follo'ws:
The urgency of action to be taken to establish a National Research Institute to promote scientific and industrial research in Canada is patent to all who know what is being done abroad in this line.
There is in Canada no organization which even distantly approaches the character of any of the research institutes established abroad or now being established.
The report then states what is being done, what has been done, and what is about to be done, in this matter, by countries like Great Britain, the United States, -Japan, and other overseas Dominions. It goes on:
It is evident, therefore, that Canada, to meet the international competition which the work of these laboratories will serve to accentuate very greatly, must have a National Research Institute, which will place at the command of the country all the resources of science and further the development of the natural wealth of the country to meet the huge burden of debt imposed by the war. The developed wealth of Canada as compared with that of the United States is small. If the natural resources of the Dominions were appropriately utilized, its developed wealth might readily be as much as ten times what it is now. The conversion of our natural resources into developed wealth, however, can only be accomplished through the application to them of science of the most highly advanced type.
One example is given, among many, of what it is hoped may be accomplished by scientific research, and it would be easy to instance others of equal importance. The report then states:
Tour Committee believe the first step towards providing for the research required is the establishment of a National Research Institute whose functions will be to carry on researches,
not only parallel to those of the Bureau of Standards at Washington, but such also as will assist in the development of the natural resources of the country and will promote the application of the most advanced scientific knowledge. to all lines of industrial production in Canada.
The report then sets forth just what work such an institution (would undertake. I do not propose to read that portion of the report verbatim, but in general terms I might explain that the functions of such an institute will be in the main of two kinds. In the first place it will he charged with the standardization of measures throughout the country, including in 'that term (a) standards of length, volume, weight, etc., of heat, light, electricity and other forms cf energy; (b) of scientific and technical apparatus whether used in the public service or in the industries of the country; and (c) of the quality of the materials required in the construction of public works and of the supplies needed in the various branches of the Government service.
The second function of the institute will be to direct and supervise researches into technical processes and methods so as to assist, first, in the development of the natural resources of Canada; second, in the expansion of existing industries or the furthering of new industries; third, in utilization of those materials which have hitherto been discarded as waste products. To put it shortly, the institute is not only to be a bureau of standards in the narrower significance of the term, but it will as well undertake the supervision of scientific industrial research for the benefit of the country at large.
The methods to be followed in the falfil-ment of the latter part of the programme will be in the main those already adopted by Great Britain and the United States. An endeavour will be made-nor do I see any reason why it should fail

to form in this country trade associations or, as it is proposed to call them, trade guilds, for research. That is to say, the industries scattered throughout the land that are interested in some form of activity will be brought together, and through their joint efforts and subscription a competent scientific investigator or research expert will be selected and his salary paid by the guild. This man and his assistants will be allotted a properly equipped laboratory in the governmental central research institute where he will find at his disposal not merely the various mechanical and physical appliances with which the institute will be furnished, but as well the skilled experience

and advice of the Government experts in charge of the institute. As I have stated, the plan outlined is that already followed in Great Britain and the United States. In the former country indeed the government is inclined to deal more liberally with the industries than our plan suggests because under the plan adopted by Great Britain, there is supplied out of the public funds to trade associations for research an equal amount to any sum which these associations can themselves raise. The report concludes with the following recommendation :
Your Committee accordingly recommend:
(1)	that a National Research Institute for Canada, endowed with the function and of the character indicated in the foregoing, be established in the vicinity of Ottawa on a site fifty acres in area of easy access and conveniently located for water, gas and electric power supply.
(2)	that the first building to be erected for the Institute should be of the best modern construction suitable for laboratory work and of such dimensions as to provide accommodation for some years to come.
(3)	that there be appropriated by Parliament $50 0/0 00 for the purchase of the site and the construction of the building, $ 100,(KM) for the scientific equipment of the Institute, and $50,-OO'O for salaries and maintenance during the first year of operation.
(4)	that legislation be enacted at this session to provide for the establishment of this National Research Institute and the government of the same.
I do not propose to discuss clause by clause these recommendations, but lest the sums mentioned might at first blush appear large, let us say to our Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), particularly in view of the need for stringent economy recognised and adopted by the Government, permit me to say that 'these figures were not reached without mature consideration. They are based in the first place on the information given to the committee last year by the director of the Bureau of Standards in the United States, and, taking into account the increased cost of building material, they practically agree with the initial expenditure made in Washington some twenty years ago for the same purpose. The figures are further confirmed by the plans and estimates prepared by a competent architect and by the judgment of those whose knowledge of such matters can be relied upon. It may be pointed out that the expenditure of the amounts mentioned must of necessity be spread over a term of years. It will be quite impossible to erect the building required and instal the equipment within the present financial year. So far as the item for salaries and maintenance is concerned, the greater part of it must remain in abeyance until the

institute is completed and is actually in operation. It is believed by the committee that the expenditure proposed will provide for the requirements of scientific research in Canada for some years to come, and it is our opinion that it would be shortsighted to make the common mistake of failing to recognize the inevitable expansion which must take place in a movement of this kind.
May I note in passing that one of the distinguished witnesses who appeared before the committee last year namely, Professor McLennan of Toronto, expressed disappointment at the meagreness of the budget which this committee has suggested and contrasted it disadvantageous^ with the infinitely more liberal provisions which the British Government has made for the same purpose since the war.
I do not propose to discuss at this stage any of the alternative suggestions which have come before the committee. They were earnestly considered and much of the testimony introduced last year bore directly on the point. The conclusion of the committee was definite, that the plan now recommended is undoubtedly the best; but I do not wish to be understood as saying that in future some qualifications of this plan may not be wise. So far as one can see, a central research institute will always be a necessity, although as in other departments there must, and I should think would be, a natural growth. If in the course of the debate questions arise in regard to alternative proposals, doubtless they can be dealt with by other speakers, or I shall be happy to take them up when I have an opportunity of closing the debate.
As before stated, the committee during last session heard evidence of a number of expert witnesses both from this country and from the neighbouring republic. These men were experts, some of whom had spent their entire lives in scientific research. While that testimony and reference to such works as are available on the subject convinced me personally of the wisdom of the proposal, it seemed wise to make a personal investigation so that I could look more closely into the actual working of institutions similar to the one proposed. With that end in view I took advantage of the late Easter vacation to pay a visit to Washington to see the Bureau of Standards, and to 'Pittsburgh to examine the Mellon Institute; and with your permission, Mr. Speaker,- I should like briefly to repeat the impressions gained by that visit, impressions which have already been conveyed to the committee.

The Bureau of Standards is situated a few miles out of Washington close to the electric line, in the centre of what has become a. well-settled residential district. The purchase made twenty years age was of eight acres. Since that time other portions surrounding the original area have been bought and the total hoMing is noiw 36 acres. This area is considered too small for the needs of the bureau, bult unfortunately the territory surrounding it has 'been largely built up and the prioe ef land has reached an extraordinarily high level. The original building is encircled by others of larger dimensions which are devoted to the evergrowing need's of the Bureau, and during the war the United States Government erected a building larger than any of those that had previously gone up. This was intended to be used for some specific war purpose but it had not been occupied at the time the Armistice was signed and the President of the United States thereupon handed it over to the Bureau. The building is of the finest factory construction, of steel and reinforced concrete and with maximum window space. It cost in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000. It hah been dedicated by the Bureau of Standards to Scientific Industrial Research and the greater part of it is already occupied by various industries or associations with a view to solving their problems-problems which constantly confront all those in the modern industrial world.
The annual estimates of the Bureau, which were considered a few weeks ago, are over $2,000,000 a year. It is true that there is some disposition this year on the part of the Houses of Congress, owing to the nearness of the presidential election, to exercise a sporadic economy by lopping off a certain amount of these estimates, but it is n'ot thought that the activities of the Bureau will be .seriously prejudiced by what, after all, is a temporary political movement. 'The original function of the Bureau was to determine standards throughout the United States. If we change but one word in the report now before the House-that is delete the word "Canada" -we have a complete description of the activities of the Bureau on its standards side. I do not propose to read a list of these activities to you. I think I have discussed theim in speaking of our own institute, but among ithem I might mention that the Bureau tests everything purchased by the Government; indeed, it goes farther 'and at the request of the various departments, it prepares specifications of all important materials which are to be purchased for the use of the public iservioe. One or two instances of this kind might be illuminating. The American Government desired to purchase incandescent lamps. Upon investigation by the Bureau it was found that the lamp supplied by the lowest tenderer was deficient in certain qualities. As a result of this inquiry the Bureau definitely established a type of lamp which would give the maximum of light and the greatest length of service. What happened? The wide-awake manufacturers in the United States were only too glad to supply that type of lamp and to secure from the Bureau a certificate as to (their quality.
Again, the Government there required, as we do in this country, vast quantities of paper for use in the public service. The , usual specification set out the materials that the paper should consist of. But when the first shipment came in the Bureau found that the paper supplied lacked entirely one of the necessary ingredients. In this case the manufacturer candidly .admitted that he had not tried to live up to the specification because he never dreamed that such a test would be made. He prepared himself at once to give exactly what the Government needed and called for.
The Bureau of Standards investigated on behalf of the Government, the question of storage batteries. They found, as a result of their scientific research into the question, that without expense the ordinary type of battery could be improved by at least ten per cent. The manufacturers, of course, were glad to adopt that improvement and it is now general throughout the whole country. When we consider that $100,000,000 worth of these batteries are each year sold throughout the country, it is perhaps not unfair to credit the Bureau ol Standards with a saving to the country oi something akin to $10,000,000. As a matter of record that research is still going on in the Bureau and the expert in charge is reasonably hopeful that he may improve the ordinary storage battery by at least 25 per cent over the one found on the commercial market.
With reference to the matter of testing materials supplied to the Government, one can understand the vast quantity of articles like cement, steel, brick and so forth that are used in that country and the statement is made by the officers of the Bureau that the saving of the Government on that one item alone is sufficient to pay the entire cost of the maintenance of the Bureau. Any manufacturer in the United

States is -at liberty to submit his wares to be tested at the Bureau of Standards and to receive an official certificate as to their quality. I think we can understand how rapidly improvements along many lines must follow because of this rule. Indeed, some Canadian firms are alive to the advantage and so far have been permitted to submit their goods to the tests of the Bureau of Standards at Washington.
Let me revert for a moment again to the question of paper. The Bureau has installed in one of the buildings a small paper mill and there it manufactures paper for all ordinary uses from the most unpromising material. The Bureau tests the ropes used in the navy, and it also tests the twine used in the various departments. It accumulates thus a great quantity of samples, and instead, of throwing these away or selling them to the ragman it converts them into paper. I have a sample of the wrapping paper used by the Government and made from manila rope. Certainly, to any one handling it, it seems to be a first-class article of its kind. They have also made paper out of stranger material than that, because I have a sample of paper made from the banana stalks of plants grown in Siam, made at the request of the representative of Siam. That paper might be very well used for various purposes, such as wrapping fruit, as it has a silky quality. There is also a paper made from a wild grass that grows in that same country-grass which to my mind is precisely like that which grows very freely in the marshes of our western provinces.
There is even a further extension of the standard side of this Bureau because the acceptance of the word "standard" has been enlarged to include standards of practice, and, following that line, standards of safety have been developed, and in co-operation with various states of the Union and municipalities these have been largely accepted throughout the whole Republic. I have under my hand one of the safety codes of standards adopted by the Bureau. It is dated 1916, and is called "The National Electric Safety Code." Now it is said, but I cannot vouch for it, that each year in the United States approximately 1,000 people meet their death by accident with electric appliances. If the use of this code, which sets out in great detail all the necessary precautions which should be taken, is adopted by the States in framing their legislation, or by the municipalities in framing their regulations, so wanton a loss of life may largely be avoided. I note that in the

introduction of this code the following paragraph appears:
The bureau has had the cordial co-operation and assistance of many state industrial and public-service commissions, municipal electrical inspectors, engineers of operating and manufacturing companies, committees of engineering societies, and representatives of the fire and casualty insurance interests, and of the electrical workers. Without such co-operation the work would have been impossible.
Similar codes dealing with the various uses of gas, with fire prevention and fire-resisting construction have been published and many others are under way. So much for the standard side of the Bureau.
Last year when Dr. Stratton, director of the Bureau, appeared before our committee, he told us something of the industrial research which was carried on in that institution. I must confess, I was greatly impressed by the very active development which has occurred along that line. This, in part, is due to the acquisition of the new building to which reference has already been made, but also in part it is due to the general recognition throughout the United States of the immense value to the country of concerted effort in scientific research. There is established at Washington a National Research Council, which, although not a governmental institution, acts in close co-operation with the various scientific departments of the government. One of its main activities is to educate industries throughout the country as to what may be accomplished by scientific research, and to counsel, by personal addresses and printed matter, through its energetic secretary and other officers, all those who might be interested. As a result there is brought prominently before the public the full meaning and significance of the movement. It should not be surprising, therefore, that full advantage has been taken of the facilities offered by the Bureau of Standards, as the industries are free to bring their problems to the Bureau and to have them investigated with the aid of the best material, both physical and mental, which the country can supply. Experience has shown that even bitter rivals in their particular line find the value of co-operation; and we were given ocular demonstration of tests being made of various methods to demonstrate which was the most effective and economical.
The Mellon Institute of Pittsburg is a pioneer institution 'in purely industrial scientific research. While its building was erected and its overhead expense of $60,000 a year is sup-

plied through the munificence of the Mellon Bros., the institution itself is conducted on a commercial basis, i.e., the parties desirous of taking advantage of its facilities must pay a fixed sum for a year or term of years. The discoveries made by means of the research accrue to the subscriber-or donor as he is termed- although as a rule liberal rewards by way of bonus are granted to the investigator who produces the result. The most striking testimony to the success of the institution is found in the fact that not only is every square foot of their large building occupied, but there is a waiting list of considerable length of those who are desirous of taking advantage of the institution. The institution has published a list of the researches undertaken by it during the past year. These are forty-eight in number, and I would like to mention a few of them to show how varied are the matters inquired into. The first one mentioned is window-glass, the next soap, then dental products, copper, oil, yeast-for which $15,000 is paid for investigation and there is a separate one for bread involving a payment of $10,000 per annum-household utilities, fuel, by-products recovery, insecticides-which has been- in existence for some years-fertilizer, laundry -in connection with this we met two young lady scientists who had been in charge of the work for some time-and the last on the list is .fruit beverages-hon. gentlemen will see they were anticipating the arid spell which has fallen on the United States. I have quoted at some length from the results of this visit, not because the institutions are American, but because they are nearby and are in line with those we desire to adopt.
It seemed well to give to the House the above sketch of the result of a trip taken with the sole view of ascertaining what could be learned of the actual operation and results of institutions similar to the one suggested for Canada. Many of us, Mr. Speaker, possess in imagination, far up the broad river of Time, an Island of Long Ago. To us it appears a delectable land where life had more of content and leisure than we can expect to gain this side of the grave. I suspect, however, that the mists of the past hide from us most of what was objectionable in that far-off region. H G. Wells may well be right when he exclaims:
" That large, naked, virtuous, pink natural man, drinking pure spring water, eating the fruits of the earth, and living to 90 in the open air, is a fantasy; he never was nor will be. . .	. The real savage is a nest of parasites
within and without; he smells, he rots, he
starves."
Whatever may be the truth in this respect is but a matter of academic interest, for the world has definitely turned its steps into the highway of national progress. As this morning's paper puts it:
Do you really want the " good old days '' when there were no Pullmans, fast trains, anaesthetics, telephones, bicycles, automobiles, moving pictures, self-binders, hay-loaders, cream-separators, phonographs, cold storage, plate glass, gas cooking ranges, incandescent lights, aeroplanes, elevators, fast ocean liners, X-ray photography, typewriters, adding machines, cash registers, asphalt, microscopes, telescopes, linotypes, high-speed presses, and automatic machines in almost every branch of endeavour? Think it over. Have these things not added something to the measure of human happiness?
If we were to examine the above heterogeneous list or any other which might be compiled we would discover that without science not a single one of the many articles mentioned would be in existence. The world, as I .say, has determined on "Progress," as its motto. Other nations are moving forward. Can we in Canada afford to neglect the systematic study of the greatest aid to advancement? Assuredly unless we make the effort we shall be left behind.
I am glad to believe that neither business life nor, what is perhaps more trying, political experience, has wholly atrophied my faculty of imagination-one need not, in a country such as ours, give even free rein to this faculty to visualize the possibilities which may be disclosed by concerted effort in scientific research. While, however, I may have exercised my imagination I have, nevertheless, endeavoured throughout the inquiry to look at this matter . from a cold-blooded business point of view. I have not the slightest hesitation in saying that from that point alone the establishment of a Central Besearch Institute will be a paying venture. Had I the resources at my disposal I would conceive it to be a thoroughly sound and profitable investment, provided the value of the discoveries and improvements made by means of .such an institute could accrue to my personal advantage.
I have attempted, Mr. Speaker, to refrain from repetition of what I said on this subject nearly a year ago. On that occasion I made the endeavour to cover a wider field; but while the temptation was pressing, I hoped that those hon. members who are interested in the subject might remember something of what was then said and would quite properly resent the threshing of old

straw. I do venture, however, once more, to repeat that the need of such an institute is pressing, that the rewards to the country will be great, and that the expenditure proposed is, in my opinion, amply justified.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of seconding the motion which has been so well proposed by the chairman of this Research Committee, my hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn). I think you will agree with me after hearing what he has said that the committee appointed by the House has not followed this inquiry in any haphazard way. Both last session and this session, but particularly last session, the committee had the privilege of hearing distinguished scientists on various questions which it desired to consider in connection with the Institute of Research.
Pioneering is, of course, expensive in all industries, and the committee has had the benefit of the experience gained in European countries and in the United States with regard to the Bureau of Standards and the Institute of Research. I am satisfied that if our country is to take its proper place in the industrial world both of these institutions are necessities for Canada in an industrial sense.
Probably at no period in the history of man has it been easier to demonstrate the value of applied science than it is to-day. The late war has amply shown us what science can do in the field; and the industrial progress of the great nations to-day shows us what the application of science is doing in connection with the industries of the world. I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that that nation which is best equipped with scientific knowledge, scientific apparatus, and scientific institutions will, in the future, have the best chance in the race for industrial supremacy or, indeed, in that of war.
Canada is rich in natural resources-immensely rich; but in order to transmute these resources into commodities which the world needs one thing particularly is required, and that is applied science. Industry you must have-you must have the intelligent artisan; you must have people in the country who have faith enough in its future to put their capital into manufacturing enterprises; but without science that labour and those manufacturing enterprises would not go very far.
My hon. friend (Mr. Cronyn) has given you very clearly the objects which the committee had in mind in recommending that a Bureau of Standards be established, and

in conjunction with it an Institute for Scientific Research. I shall not traverse again the ground that he so well covered, but I would like to refer to just one or two items, particularly in connection with the Bureau of Standards. Take for instance, Mr. Speaker, our unit of measurement, the yard. It had its origin in the mists of antiquity, came across the Channel with the Anglo-Saxons, and now the representative of that system is lying somewhere in the archives of the city of London in the shape of a metal bar of a certain length. In 1870 the French people decided to create a new unit of measurement, and they took a section of a quadrant of the circumference of the earth and called it a metre. It was not very many years before the scientific men of their country discovered that the metre was not scientifically accurate. Since then scientists have discovered a means whereby a measurement can be adopted which is universal and never-changing-the wave of light; and 1 have no doubt that within the next few years that will be the standard of measurement for length. So I might refer to the unit for the measure of volume and other units of measurement, but I will not detain the House in regard to them.
My hon. friend has referred to the testing of building material-a very excellent thing for us to have to-day-in connection with our public works-in order to ascertain the strength and quality of such materials. I do not think our Government have any means at the present time of making such tests.
With regard to research, it is well known that we have huge areas of tar sands in the northern and western portions of our Prairie Provinces. They have been there for millions of years; they will be there for millions of years longer unless we can discover some means of taking from them their asphaltic products and transferring them to the markets of the world. There is therefore a great field for research in relation to those tar sands. So too with iron ore. We were told here the other day that the higher grades of iron ores are being depleted and that soon we shall have to depend on the low grade ores of Canada- another field for scientific research.
We are about to enter the world as an exporting trade nation, and it is absolutely necessary that our goods when exported should bear the hallmark of quality; otherwise these three transcontinental roads we have built and these great merchant ships we are putting on the oceans of the world

will not carry the cargoes from our shores that they should carry. Therefore I hope that when this Bureau of Standards is established in Ottawa every ton of goods leaving Canada will bear the stamp of that Bureau which will mean Canadian quality of the first class.
I was interested a few days ago to meet a man who told me that our greatest competitors in the sale of wheat in the Liverpool market were the Russians. He informed me that the Russian wheat was sold in Liverpool by sample; the Canadian wheat was sold by standard. And it was easier to sell the Canadian wheat, and it brought a little better price.
In this great province of Ontario, Mr. Speaker, there is not one ton of coal-hard coal, soft coal or lignites; and to-day when coal prices are pressing so heavily upon us it is very important, and it will become increasingly important, to find relief from this burden. We have billions of tons of coal east of us, and we have billions of tons of coal west of us, but in this the greatest province, the richest province, the most populous province, there is not one ton of coal. Now, underlying the western provinces there are billions of tons of lignite, which, our scientists tell us, can be transformed into coal almost equal to the Pennsylvania anthracite coal,-and that coal is within our own country. What an excellent thing it would be if the money that we are now sending, and will send, to the United States for hard coal could be kept within Canada; could be used in the purchase of the anthracite which now lies beneath our western prairies. I have no doubt that within a few years this will take place, because its practicability has already been demonstrated.
Potash is one of the things which we must have if we are to continue as an agricultural nation. Potash is one of the great things which made it possible for Germany to raise the field products which she raised, immense salt deposits have recently been discovered in Nova Scotia, and there are other salt deposits throughout Canada. There is some potash in these salt deposits. It is possible, therefore, that we shall be able to develop the potash industry within our own country.
Electric smelting is only in its infancy. If it were possible to harness the great water-powers of our country and smelt the iron ores to which I referred a few minutes ago, we would keep more than one hundred million dollars of good Canadian money within Canada. Go down to the lumber
sections of our country and you will see thousands upon thousands of tons of sawdust banked in the river valleys and wherever saw mills have been or are situated- absolutely going to waste. Now, any scientific man will tell you that that sawdust is a great potential asset; all that is required is the scientific knowledge to tackle the problem and to take from that material some of the commodities which it contains and which we could use. If we had a research institute in this country, with men, with money, and with the necessary apparatus, we could accomplish great work along this line.
The explosive engine has revolutionized traffic. Without the explosive engine you could not have automobiles; without it you could have no aerial navigation; without it no aeroplane could rise into space. But the explosive engine is almost altogether, if not entirely, dependent upon gasoline. Any person who has studied this question will tell you that, according to the opinion of scientific men of the United States, the end of the deposits of petroleum in that country is already in sight. I have not a doubt in my mind that within the lifetime of men who are now within the sound of my voice, the petroleum deposits of the United States will have become exhausted. What then? Some other fuel will have to take the place of petroleum, or gasoline, one of its products. What fuel is most likely to do that? Industrial alcohol. Here is a great field for our research institute.
The oil shales of Canada offer another field for research and experiment. Billions of tons of oil shale from which petroleum can be extracted may be found in the Maritime Provinces. Or, we have still another resource-straw, which is now being burned every year on our prairies, can be transmuted into gas which can be used for power.
We are trying to establish in this country the flax industry. Science, applied to that industry, by cultivating germs which will be placed in tanks with the flax fibre may hasten the retting process and make it possible to produce flax more cheaply, as we must do if we are to compete with the Irish and Belgian products. So with fish refuse -and I might go on indefinitely, but I shall not do so.
I wish to refer, before closing, to a few things that science has done. I shall not elaborate upon what Watt did in the development of steam; Farraday in the development of electricity; Pasteur in the

application of science to the development of the silkworm industry in France, and to the destroying of a disease which killed the sheep of France many years ago. Then we have Graham Bell with the telephone and Kelvin with the compass; and we have wireless telegraphy. iNot long ago an American magazine asked its readers to give them a synopsis of what they considered to be the seven wonders of the modern world. From the replies to these inquiries the following were selected as the seven wonders of the modern world:	Wireless
telegraphy, the telephone, the aeroplane, radium, antiseptics, antitoxins, and the seventh was divided between spectrum analysis and X-rays. All of these, Mr. Speaker, with the exception of antiseptics- even that was introduced not many decades ago-have come into being within our own lifetime.
We have heard a great deal about the paper industry; about what a wonderful thing the pulp industry is in our own country. Do you know how that industry originated? A French naturalist named Beamur was one day walking through the fields of France when he observed a wasp's nest constructed of paper and like material produced by the insects by the mastication of wood fibre and other substances. The naturalist had the imagination to see that this material could be used as paper, and from that simple observation has arisen the whole pulp industry of the world. This gives you a slight idea, Mr. Speaker, of the possibilities of science.
Then, take calcium carbide, the discoverer of which, Mr. Wilson, lived for years in our city. Calcium carbide produces acetylene gas. Many parts of our coasts are lighted with acetylene gas; the miners use acetylene gas in the lamps which they carry in their hats.
A few years ago a girl in Colorado was washing some ore sacks in which ore belonging to her brother had been carried. She noticed in the soap suds some small particles of metal floating on the bubbles. She told that to a scientist; the scientist developed the idea, and to-day you have tha flotation process throughout the length and breadth of this land and in the United States as well.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, permit me to qhote from Buckle as to the value of science, scientific men and scientific ideas:
The discoveries of great men never leave us ; they are immortal. They contain those eternal truths which survive the shock of empires, outlive rival creeds and witness the decay of suc-
[Mr. A. Thompson. 1
cessive religions. To the discoveries of genius we owe all that we now have; they are for all ages and all times; never young, never old, they bear the seeds of their own life ; they flow on in a perennial stream ; they are essentially cumulative and thus influence posterity and after the lapse of centuries produce more effect than they were able to do even at the moment of their promulgation.

Mr. Speaker, I am fully sensible of the difficulties which the subject now under discussion presents, and were it not for my desire, as a member of the committee which is now reporting to the House, to contribute in my humble way to the discussion, I should certainly have abstained from adressing the House on this occasion.
I offer my compliments to the chairman of the committee for the splendid work which he has accomplished in connection with the subject of the resolution now before the House, which, if adopted, will result in the carrying on of a work of great benefit to the country. This is a question into which politics do not enter at all. It is a question upon which every member can feel perfectly free to express his opinion. What is asked is that a national research institute be established in Canada in order to promote scientific and industrial research generally, which includes a great many subjects, as has been pointed out by the mover of the resolution (Mr. Cronyn). To the casual observer it might appear that this project is a luxury, a sport, something of purely academic interest; but such is not the ease. Now the war is over we have to cope with the afterwar conditions, and we must not lose sight of the fact that since the war, and even during the war, the different nations of the world have entered upon a wild race to capture the trade of the world and the predominant position in commerce. Even while the war was on and the battlefields of Europe were soaked with blood, the nations had the foresight to appreciate that immediately the war was over this race for the world's trade would be begun. The United States were in a peculiarly advantageous position in this respect, because they only entered the war in its last year practically, and thus were enabled to make preparations which the other nations that had been engaged in the war from the beginning were unable to make. From the report of the Special Committee on Scientific Research we see that Great Britain, France, Italy, the Commonwealth of Australia, New Zealand, the United States, Germany, and Japan, in fact practically all the civilized nations of the world, have re-

cognized since the war is over, or had recognized before the war, the necessity of scientific research in promoting the trade and commerce of their respective countries. Before the war Germany perhaps more than any other nation had travelled in the fields of scientific research, and that is one of the reasons why, rightly or wrongly, she was looked upon as the land of culture. Germany had astonished the world with her marvellous inventions, and it is not too much to say that through her .many inventions she had achieved the prosperity through which she was passing when she declared war on the world. Her success in invention continued through the early stages of the war, and in fact all through it. We all remember how, in the month of April, 1915, suddenly 'and without warning, Germany developed that great gas attack which heralded a new phase in the war. Of course, the use of gas was strictly forbidden by all the rules of war, and no civilized nation had ever attempted to use it up to that time, but the fact remains that Germany had in her possession secrets which the other nations did not possess, or at all events, not to the same extent. We all remember how when these poisonous gases were let loose on our armies, the Allies could noit find out their exact composition, but immediately scientists began investigating and determined their composition, and in order to offset the unlawful advantage which Germany had thereby gained the Allies in turn were compelled to invent and manufacture new gases to be used against the German armies. They had also to invent appliances to resist the gases by which they were attacked. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, where would the Allies have been at that time of perplexity if they had not had in their midst scientists and scientific institutions that could devote themselves at once to a study of these gases and devise a protection against them? Germany did other things. We know that before the war she had practically a monopoly of the incomparable dyes which she was selling to the whole civilized world. That is surprising, because one would naturally have expected England to be the place where these [DOT]dyes were manufactured. In the field of war Germany also had her Zeppelins, her submarines, and that wonderful cannon with a range of 75 miles with which she bombarded Paris in the forever-famous offensive of March, 1918. All through the war Germany brought out new inventions from time to time, and these inventions were so numerous and called into being so many devices on our side in order to coun-138
teract them that General Joffre is reported to have said after leaving his army for three or six months he would not be able to lead them any more because he had not kept abreast of the many new developments in warfare.
Germany not only had marvellous inventions of destruction, but her scientific institutions were so advanced that she would have been able to capture the trade of the world had she not committed the blunder of declaring war and trying to subdue mankind by force of arms. The civilized world to-day is determined that no nation shall be allowed to repeat the attempt which Germany launched in 1914, and it i.s generally recognized now that if trade is to be gained it must be not through war but through peaceful methods, by the development Of indnstries, the intensive prosecution of agriculture, and the exploitation of every resource which a progressive nation can make use of.
And this is just where the question of scientific research becomes important. We are not asking for the establishment of an institution to destroy humanity as the Germans did; we are trying to produce wealth for the benefit of the nation. I hope there will be no serious objection to the proposal now before us, but if there is it can only be in relation to the financial considerations involved. It might be argued that while the proposal is one that is well worthy of consideration there is not sufficient means to take any practical steps in the matter. Well, so far as this objection is concerned, I ithink every hon. member will realize that scientific research is neither a luxury nor a sport; nor is it a subject of purely academic interest. As was said a moment ago by 'the mover of the resolution, scientific research is a cold-blooded business proposition, and the motion which is under consideration is nothing if ndt extremely practical. Our public delbt is enormous and we say that we do not know how we shall make ends meet; and some hon. members might conclude that as our expenditures are so high at the present time it is not advisable to give effect to the recommendations which have been made in this matter. Well, Sir, I isay that the public debt is certainly enormous-, and we are confronted with a great problem to provide the necessary revenue. But from the premises I draw an altogether different conclusion. If we are ever going to discharge the public debt of this country our only hope lies in the development of our natural resources This is the only way in which we shall b s able



to pay the huge debt we incurred during the war, and this proposed institute fof scientific research, far from adding to the burdens which we already have to hear, will, I am sure, prove a valuable asset, and the benefits that will accrue from its operation will more than offset the expenditures that may be made fen connection with it. The Government has recently undertaken a shipbuilding programme which is costing us something like $60,000,000. Whatever objections there may be to this undertaking, a majority of the members of this House have expressed their beliel that Ithe expenditure of this $60,000,000 on ships will be a benefit to the country. We have also acquired the property of the Grand Trunk Bailway Company. The debate on that subject was long, and although we on this side of the House pronounced against the transaction, nevertheless a majority of the members regarded this matter also as beneficial to the Canadian nation, and evidently they believe that the expenditure of $500,000,000 will prove a very wise one. A year or two ago Canada lent considerable sums of money to Bon mania, Greece and other foreign states, and this is a matter that is open to very much debate; very diverse views may be held in regard to it; hut the fact remains that the Government considered it a sound policy and one that would he advantageous to the people of Canada to lend money to those countries. I cite these stupendous undertakings in order to show that the question of money is not the most serious obstacle. The question is nolt: What expenses will he involved in the new institution?-but: What revenue will the country derive from its operation? A convincing answer to this question was given in the eloquent speech made by the mover of the resolution, and no1 one who heard that speech could fail to realize what an enormous advantage the establishment of a Scientific Research Institute must be. I shall not attempt to go into details; one could only touch a few of the multitude of questions that would arise in the consideration of this subject. This proposed institution could deal with an infinitude- of matters. As an example we might take the exploitation of our coal fields, as mentioned a moment ago. At this time, when we are paying $1.10 for every dollar's worth of goods we buy in the United States, we are actually buying from that country coal to the amount of $70,000,000 a year. If through the process of scientific research we could find a way by which our soft coal -in Canada, of which we have an immeasureable 
quantity, could be utilized, if but partly, in place of the coal which we now import from the United States, through this item alone the expenditure which this new bureau might involve would be repaid tenfold.
I wish once more to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for London for the magnificent work he has done. I would not take the responsibility of saying that he has been the only man in this country who ever thought of having a Bureau of Scientific Research. Others probably have had the same idea, but he has the merit-the great merit-of being the first member of this House to take this question into his own hands, to follow it up, and to give his whole time to it.
I am aware that he even went to the United States to make a personal study of the matter. The hon. member, with the knowledge and accomplishments that we all know him to possess, was convinced from the outset that such a scheme could only be beneficial to the country, and, being anxious to serve his country, he has spared neither time nor effort to accomplish what is now before the House.
I say therefore, Sir, that I hope this House will find itself unanimous on this point. I am only speaking for myself, hut from what I can see my friends on this side of the House are warm on this subject and are ready to endorse it.. From what I can see members on the other side of the House are ready to support the motion, and it would be a great satisfaction, I am.sure, for my hon. friend from London, this House, and the country generally, if we could say to-night that the House had accepted unanimously the motion which is now under consideration.

in Canada. When you consider that the whole fishing industry of the Dominion only represents a value of about $40,000,000, and that the value of the waste products alone is $10,000,000, you can see how science applied to an industry of that kind may have very profitable results.
I might also instance the baking industry to show the value of scientific research. A scientist in the United States, in seeking substitutes for sugar in the yeast, made a discovery which nets one firm over there no less than half a million dollars a year, and they were so appreciative of the fact that they gave the discoverer a gratuity of no less than $35,000.
We are also told that in the perfecting of what is called the tungsten lamp we have an annual saving in electrical power of over $2,000,000,000. These are instances of discoveries which, when applied to the great industries of this country, or any country, may produce a great monetary reward.
Another example I might mention is that of the great glass industry of the United .'States. Potash salts were used in connec-lion with this industry, supplies of which were obtained from Germany. When war broke out that source of supply was cut off and it was thought for a time that the industry would be paralysed. However, they got their scientists to work and very shortly they produced a substitute and the industry was able to carry on its operations.
I might go on enumerating case after case where the application of science has been, and is to-day, of very great material value to the industries of this country. Up to the present time, Canada has no research institutions-we have practically been living off the brains of the world. I hope the Government will take this fact very seriously into consideration and give to our industries the advantages that they should have in order to enable them to compete with the other industries of the world. We have great natural resources in Canada with almost unlimited possibilities. We have, for example, as has been referred to already to-night, the important pulp industry, from which has been developed your great cellulose industry. Cellulose, I might say, is the basic product in the cell structure of all vegetable life, and without it you would have no food for either animal or man. Now, it has been found that by treating our pulpwood with caustic soda, pulp is produced. That treated with sulphates and sulphites under pressure produces other material. For example, the

artificial silk industry has its basis there. We find that industry producing an article which takes on very intensive dyes, and this artificial silk industry in the United States was worth last year no less than $35,000,000. The treating of cellulose with nitric acid produce nitro-cellulose compounds, which were so important to us during the war. One could go on endlessly with the discoveries in connection with different industries-discoveries which may possibly result in increasing our wealth almost beyond our dreams.
Another example I might mention is the treatment of the waste products of the sawmill and the pulp mill by utilizing an experiment which was made by a scientist many years ago. This scientist found that by treating some old linen with sulphuric acid he produced a species of sugar, and by the fermentation of that sugar we get ethyl alcohol. By using the liquor from the pulp mills and the sawdust from the sawmills, we get ethyl alcohol which sells to-day at $7 a gallon. A load of sawdust, worth only 50 or 75 cents, will yield 10 gallons of ethyl alcohol, 95 per cent in strength, and a bushel of grain,-worth, roughly speaking, $1.50-will produce about two and a quarter gallons. Hon. gentlemen will therefore see the possibilities of science when applied to any industry. I could go on for an hour giving examples of how science applied to one industry and another will produce untold wealth.
I hope that the Government will delay no longer in establishing this Research Council and providing it with thoroughly equipped buildings and adequate help. I am glad to bear witness to-night to the efficiency of the gentleman at the head of the council, who has made a world-wide reputation through research. I know personally that he has refused the presidency of no less than five universities, and was asked to put in an application for the Chair of Physiology in the great University of Glasgow. I think we are fortunate indeed in having a man of his calibre to organize and direct this Research Council. I hope the Government will support him and accord that support at once. It is only by making practical application of the discoveries made by scientists that the industries of Canada can reap the benefit of them and the country can attain its proper status among the commercial nations of the world.

It
ought not to be hard for any hon. gentleman here to support the motion for the adop-

tion of this report. Time will not permit the mention of more than one or two of the many reasons why one is particularly interested in the proposed establishment of a Bureau of Standards and a Research Institute for the Dominion of Canada at the present time. Some Canadian people may think that the greater universities in our country should care for this work. It is not their function to do this form of work. They are not financially conditioned to provide the equipment. It is for them to furnish the researchers who will be selected, if an institute of this kind is established by the Government, and who will bring to their respective university mothers fame and distinction because of the further work which they carry on-not to show their scholastic attainments and their ability as discoverers but to show their capacity for furthering the development of the great natural resources of our country of which so much is being said in these days but for the scientific development of which so little is being done.
We are not trespassing in any way upon the field of university educational endeavour ; we are doing that which .Canada should do in its own interests. May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that Canada will need in the next generation enough researchers to introduce the great principles of conservation in connection with the carrying out of purpose, (f) as contained in the report submitted by the chairman of the committee (Mr. Cronyn). That purpose is described to he:
Researches undertaken to promote the utilization of the waste products of industry.
Our wealth will be greatly increased if we are prepared to convert the millions otf dollars' worth of waste now unreclaimed and unconserved.
The hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Me-Gibbon) has said that we have been too long trusting the brains of other parts of the world for leadership in research. And yet, Mr. Speaker, Professor McLennan-a most distinguished witness before the Special Committee of last session-told us of the magnificent qualifications of graduates of our Canadian universities who assisted him, an employee of the British Government, on the war-time research work of a most important character; and as a result of the work done by him, assisted by these young researchers, practical scientific young men, the enemy was handled in a way that otherwise would have been impossible for months. It is even more important in times of peace that we should make provision for our sons, and our daughters, too, -who will be ready to become researchers and so aid the great industrial concerns of our country-to develop those resources and to conserve to the very best end possible those interests and that wealth which are within our reach and possession.
It may be that the day of the production of the outstanding and conspicuous genius is past; the discoverers, the releasers of new found principles may not be increased in numbers in the coming generation; but Canada has already demonstrated that she is capable of producing young men and women who, if given the opportunity, are abundantly able to make use of the discoveries already at hand and so to recombine them that practical results will easily be within the range of attainment.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker that we all hope that the Government will very favourably consider the report that has been submitted to us by this committee for adoption.

Mr. Speaker, I promise you that I will be exceed. ingly brief-in fact, at this time of night I would not say anything at all after the very conclusive speech made by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), were it not that I feel it is advisable in the interests of our country that we rally all the support possible to the hon. member and his committee in their efforts to improve conditions in Canada.
As I see this report of the Committee of Scientific and Industrial Research, the adoption of which is moved by the member for London, the recommendation can be reduced to a very small compass indeed. They simply recommend that this Parliament establish a national brain for advising and directing that industrial expansion which we have all been so long wanting and clamouring for; they recommend that we establish a national brain for advising and directing that greater agricultural development which is so desirable; they recommend that we establish a national brain for advising and directing the development of our national resources which have been so much discussed. We have the brain power; there is no question about that. Individually we possess it; but collectively-well, we have absolutely nothing. And the purport of the proposal now is that we shall unite our people in one great national movement to secure 'the advantage of the brain power which our own people possess.
For the last two years particularly we have been clamouring for the development

Mr. Speaker, only the very great importance of this subject would seem to justify me in taking up a few minutes of the time of the House at this late hour, but at the risk of interfering with the comfort of members I wish to add to what has already been said, a few words in support of the adoption of the report of the committee which has been so ably presided over by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), and which report has been supported tonight by a number of very excellent addresses.

One of the most urgent calls to Canada to-day is to develop its vast natural resources, to reach out for the most scientific methods of using those resources in industry, and to further the utilization of the vast amount of waste products of our industries. When we begin to feel, as we have scarcely yet felt, the keen pressure of the great economic burden imposed on this young country by our participation in the great war, Canadians will have a sharp awakening and will shake off the lethargy and apathy regarding this great question. We must see that that awakening does not come too late. The world to-day is calling for our foodstuffs, our minerals and their products, our timber, and for numerous other articles which are the product of this country.
Never in past history has such a favourable time been offered for the development of our resources. The demand is urgent, prices are high. The door of national opportunity is ajar. The chance now offers for Canada to enter. We have the resources, the energy, the capital, the labour. We need science applied to the untouched stores of our national and natural wealth to transform these vast resources into actual values in order that we may the more easily bear our war burden.
The war has opened a new era, and Canada, whose day is just beginning, has more to expect from the auspicious age that is dawning for the world than almost any other nation. To achieve great things in the new peace it is as necessary to be in the highest state of preparedness as it was for achieving great things in the war.
The recent great war has been followed by a trade war. As far as possible every country is putting its industrial house in order with a view to holding its place in the coming commercial struggle. In many countries increased attention is being devoted to scientific research as an instrument of enhanced industrial power. To-day modern methods are essential to success in industry. The manufacturer rapidly recognized that pure science is a practical thing, and that science and industry are complements of each other. To the scientist at least it is very apparent that the enormously rich undeveloped resources of Canada cannot be utilized to the best advantage of the Canadian people unless our industries have the assistance of thoroughly trained scientific experts.
While the war illustrated that scientific research was of vital concern, so it will [Mr. .Steeled
demonstrate that it is in peace just as vital to the national safety. Let us for a moment look at somq of the things science did for us in this war-and I wish to add my word of praise for the splendid part played by the scientists of Canada. It is probably unknown to the Canadian people what an important part was played in the successful scientific operations of the war by the men. of scientific training who went from Canada to 'Great Britain. Prior to the recent conflict, America and Canada were supplied almost entirely by Germany with synthetic drugs and chemicals, with dye stuffs and with potash. That is all changed, and we through the efforts of our scientific experts, are now quite independent of Germany for all these products.
Take potash, for example. Until 1915, when Germany placed an embargo on potash export, the whole world was supplied from the mines in Saxony, and after the supply from Germany was stopped the price rose from $40 per ton to from $350 to $500 per ton, making it practically impossible for the. Canadian or American farmer to utilize it. This created a great need, and scientists set to work. A certain scientific man undertook to preserve* the orange groves of Southern California from destruction by dust from cement plants, and during his experiments discovered thiat cement dust contained large quantities of potash which could be extracted in quantities as great as If lb. per barrel of cement, or a total possible of 75,000 tons per year from United States and Canadian plants; thus discovering a new source of potash which supplied some of the lack. Blast furnaces also* show large quantities of potash salts in the waste gas from the furnaces. This is estimated to produce 500,000 tons per year. Potash is also obtained from kelp on the Pacific coast. There are large quantities of feldspar in Canada, which also contains more or less poltaish. AH these sources, practically utilized, have provided the means of supplying the needs of Canada with all the potash that is at present required. In that way mien p'f science overcame the meed tor German potash.
To illustrate in a more practical way the value of 'scientific research, perhaps I can choose no better method than to give some examples of what has been done, and if I quote American examples it is because they provide better illustrations than any in Canada. We can often learn from the operations of private enterprise, and these illustrations which I intend to give to the House to-night are the efforts of private

enterprise to improve their conditions through the utilization of science.
Prior to the war America produced none of the finest optical glass; that all came from Germany. When the supply was cut off the research men of Bauseh and Lomb of Rochester went to' work and produced a glass equal to the 'best previously imported.
The General Electric Company of Schenectady keeps a laboratory at an annual cost of $500,000, and employs 75 investigators, all experts. One product of this laboratory was the tungsten lamp, ithe general use of which effedtis a saving of probably several hundred millions of dollars every year in the cost of our electric lighting. To show what value this company places on scientific research, let me say thalt in 1918 this company expended $2,000,000 on research work.
Let us see what some other concerns are doing in this line of work. The Dupont Company, of Wilmington, Delaware, established a research laboratory in 1908, and in that year expended $200,000 on research work. In 1918, a war year, the company spent $2,000,000; from 1912 to 1915 they expended $1,200,000, in research; .and by so doing they claim they effected a saving oi $14,000,000. They now employ 1,100 chemists.	.
The Eastman Kodak Co. employs 40 research workers at an annual cost of $150 -
000.
The Western Electric Company, of New York, spent in 1918, a war year, $2,500,000 in research work.
A well known chemist in the United States was approached by a group of firms who had spent $100,000 on a problem without results. They told him they were willing to spend $100,000 more and to wait five years for a solution of the problem. Three research men were put to work and 'Solved the problem ait a icoist of only $2,000.
Forty years ago cotton seed by-products were a dead waste. To-day they are worth over $300,000,000 per year. The research worker did it. Now, if any private enterprise feels justified in spending large sums because returns are being obtained that warrant these expenditures and if private Concerns obtain such results from their investments and their efforts I see no reason why Canada should hesitate in embarking on work of this kind.'
Let me quote Dr. Stratton of the United States Bureau of Standards for further illustrations. He says:
If there is any one good which has come to the United States out of the war it is their scientific industrial development.
And further he says:
One of the problems of builders and architects has been to know the strength of steel required for structural work. The Bureau of Standards by actual tests established standards upon which all buildings, bridges, shipbuilding, etc., can be carried on with safety. It is estimated that in this connection the amount saved to the industries in one year by preventing faulty construction will pay for all the experimental work of the whole Bureau many times over.
Let us look at>
Canada for a moment in connection with the fuel question of this country. At this time of our country'3 history, when the fuel problem is becoming acute and when a substitute for American coal is eagerly sought, it is most gratifying to know that our own Canadian scientific workers have made very satisfactory progress in so modifying our lignites of the western provinces as to make them available for heating the homes of Western Canada. There is every prospect that in the near future the immense fields of lignite in the West will be commercially available; and thus will be solved one of the great problems of that western country at an immense industrial advantage to Canada and a vast saving to our people.
The problem in Canada to-day is very different from what it was ten years ago. There is a great deal of difference in conditions when coal is sold at $15 a ton from the conditions that existed when it was sold at $6 a ton, and this one question alone, it seems to me, is sufficient to warrant the Government in going any length and in making any expenditure in order to make available the western coal for the people of that great and growing country. Let me quote the opinion of another man on this subject. I quote him because he represents that great body of citizens of Great Britain, the Labour Unions. About one year after the beginning of the war there was issued a white paper signed by Arthur Henderson, then a member of the British Cabinet. In that is found the following:
It is impossible to contemplate without considerable apprehension the situation that will arise at the end of the war unless our scientific resources have previously been enlarged and organized to meet it.
It appears incontrovertible that if we are to advance or even maintain our industrial position we must as a nation aim at such a development of scientific and industrial research as will place us in a position to expand and strengthen our industries and to compete successfully with the most highly organized of our rivals.
I advocate the establishment in Canada of a Scientific Research Institute for two chief general reasons:

First:	We need it for the development
of our vast natural resources. Nature has been most lavish with her gifts to Canada. She makes no mistakes, but having given unto us so bountifully she expects us to utilize what she has bestowed upon us. Many of our natural resources are not easily made available for the use of our people, but one of the most powerful weapons available to man for the solution of Nature's problems is scientific research. As I said before, we require the development and large utilization of out natural resources to enable us . to more easily carry our war burden, and for that reason research has become to us a fundamental and patriotic duty which can neither be ignored nor neglected without imperilling our national welfare. It will better enable us to increase production and eliminate waste.
Second: We require such an Institute as an aid to Canadian industry. Efficiency and science must go hand in hand if industry is to attain its best place. Just as science forged the most effective weapons of the late war' so she must forge the weapons of industry. Without proper means for research our industries will be heavily handicapped in their endeavours to compete with their foreign rivals. If an American farmer reaped his crop with a self-binder and the Canadian farmer with the old-fashioned sickle the Canadian would be inviting economic death. Science is the self-hinder of the crop of industry. Let us make use of it.
There is much talk of Capital and Labour these days in connection with industry. It is gradually dawning on men's minds that there is a third force in making industry successful, viz: management.
But there is a fourth:
To these three, Capital, Labour and Management, we must now add Science.
I desire to congratulate the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) on the very excellent remarks he made to-night on this subject. As a representative of that great province, which is so rapidly advancing in industry, I believe he has given a lead to his fellow-members from Quebec on this question. It almost seems that he has a vision of the future greatness of that province as one of the large industrial centres of this country. That position, can be attained effectively and satisfactorily only through the agency of science. I am very much pleased to have heard the hon. member add his word of commendation of this plan now proposed.

In conclusion, let me say that one of the most- urgent duties of the Canadian people to-day is the application of science to the development of our natural resources and to the building up of our industries. These will bring to this country a new era of progress and prosperity.
I therefore join with those who have already spoken in urging upon the Government as strongly as I can the necessity and advisability of adopting the report and carrying out the recommendations which it has laid before the House. It is not a matter of expenditure; this is an investment which will return to the country a hundredfold all that is invested.
