speechtext: committees, while they are eminent in the various professions, and occupations in which they are engaged, are men who have been serving this country in that capacity for the last five years free of charge. They are men who have other duties to perform, they are men who cannot be expected to go into detail, and deal with each of these questions which are submitted; they can only advise the Government and, to a very limited extent, those who are engaged in these industries. I submit that, as an appreciation of the work which these men have done during the past five years, and in view of the necessities of the time, the Government should at once proceed with the establishment of this Bureau of National Research in the Dominion, and place at its disposal an appropriation which would at least enable the work to be started this year.

Inasmuch as on a former occasion,, when blaming the Government for the vast expenditure of money, I advocated the creation of a Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, I think I should be guilty of negligence to-night if I allowed the opportunity to pass without saying a few words in support of the present proposition. We know that this country is a land of most wonderful resources, the fringe of which we have scarcely more than touched. Iron is an article for which there is no substitute-which is used by everybody throughout the wide world-yet we know that we are importing ninety-five per cent of the supplies we need from foreign countries. The states of Minnesota and Michigan, and I believe Alabama, are rich in iron deposits; but in our opinion there is untold wealth in the iron ores of Ontario and Quebec as well as of the Maritime Provinces. We have schools of science to which our young men resort but to perfect themselves they go to the Massachusetts Technical School. We have in Canada enormous water-powers and great mineral and agricultural wealth. Reference has been made to the by-products of our industries and to the fact that many sources of potential wealth are at present not utilized. We need in this country a Department of Scientific Research that will minister to the needs of our young men and keep them at home. We know that during the past two months several of our brainy men have left this country-men whom we could ill afford to lose-because we could not give them adequate salaries. I believe the

patriotism and love of country which exists among our young men is such that, after they have received scientific and technical training we could retain their services could we only provide them with two-thirds of the stipend they would derive in the United States.
Attention has been drawn to-night to the use that is being made of sawdust, an article that formerly was dumped into our rivers and constituted a menace to navigation. I believe there is at present being organized in Montreal a company to work up the by-products of pulp-mills. That company, I understand, are already at work with their suction pumps and turning out a valuable commodity.
The establishment of this Bureau is a splendid move, and as a business man 1 shall support the measure. To many of us the subjects relating to science are extremely technical in their nature. For example, even in the case of well-informed men, it is easy to puzzle them by asking them to define electricity. We have no satisfactory definition of what it is; we know that it is a manifestation of nature.
I have been able to puzzle pretty brilliant men who have spent two or three years in scientific study, some of whom have graduated in science, by asking them what a kilowatt is.
In establishing this department let us go cautiously Do not let us squander money, but let us start by building upon a firm foundation. Then we can afford- the aid that will be necessary to a growing department to assist in developing the great resources of this country and the tremendous possibilities that are within our reach. I am very pleased to support the measure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
After a week of political controversy it is a somewhat pleasing experience to be able to speak, even at this late hour, upon a great national problem as to which there 'appears to be unanimity of thought and feeling Having begun the week by making a special plea to my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) to permit us to adjourn at a reasonable hour each night, I shall on the present occasion make my remarks very brief. My reason for rising is that I do not wish to let this opportunity go by without in the first place extending my congratulations to the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) for his very lucid and eloquent exposition of the report of the committee, and the exceedingly industrious, and earnest manner in which he has sought to further the committee's work, and to bring to the

attention of the Government and of Parliament the significance of the establishment of a National Research Institute for Canada. I desire also, Mr. Speaker, to lend to that project such support as a word from this side of the House may afford. One is greatly tempted-if one has any appreciation of the importance of scientific research in its relation not only ito production in industry, but also to the advancement of human well-being-to speak at considerable length upon a subject such as this; hut I shall resist the temptation except to the extent of one reference to What seems to me the significance in a large way of our consideration of this project at this particular moment. Two or three of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken this evening have referred to the great scientist, Pasteur, of the contribution which he made to industry and of how illuminating his work and his life have been in revealing, not only the service that science can render to industry, but, as I have already remarked, the service which it also renders to the advancement of human well-being. At the time of the foundation of the Pasteur Institute, in commemoration of his work, in Paris-I think it was in 1888-this great scientist was so overcome with the reception tendered him by the statesmen and scientists of France, that he gave to his son a document which he had previously prepared to read to the gathering, and in that document there appeared the following paragraph which 1 think, in a way, is epoch-marking in its significance:
" Two contrary laws seem to be wrestling with each other nowadays: the one, a law of blood and of death, ever imagining new means of destruction, and forcing nations to be constantly ready for the battlefield-the other, a law of peace, work, and health, ever evolving new means of delivering man from the scourges which beset him. The one seeks violent conquests, the other the relief of humanity. The latter places one human above any victory; while the former would sacrifice hundreds of thousands of lives to the ambition of one. Which of these two laws shall ultimately prevail, God alone knows."
Since Pasteur uttered those words, we have seen something of the operation of the law of blood and of death. We have seen something of the ambitions of a single individual which have resulted in the sacrifice of hundreds of thousands of lives. Clearly, we have now come to a time when we begin to see again the furthering in a large way of the operation of the law of peace, work and health, which seeks to relieve mankind of the burdens which oppress it and to advance human well-being and human progress.
Scientific research can be employed as the handmaid either of the forces of destruction or of those oif creation and advancement, and in this particular proposal which is feeing considered at the moment in the report which the committee has brought down there is presented to this country a project which will go far, I believe, towards a realization of the application of the law of peace, work, and health in all that pertains to our social, industrial, and commercial life. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I should be sorry to let this occasion go by without expressing the hope that the report of the committee will not only be accepted unanimously-[DOT] as it is certain to be-but also that it will be carried out as speedily as possible once it is accepted by the Government.
There is another reason why I find particular pleasure in supporting this recommendation. When I had the privilege of being Minister of Labour it was my good fortune to have the opportunity of recommending to my colleagues the appointment of a royal commission on industrial training and technical education. That commission was appointed, and as hon. members know, a very valuable report was prepared by it, one section of which is devoted to this important question of industrial research. Were one anxious to suiplement what has been said this evening in support of the importance of an Industrial Research Institute one might quote at great length from this document issued by the Government, and which has recommended the very same kind of project so well emphasized by the committee that have given this matter such careful consideration.
Therefore, with the report of the Royal Commission and with the unanimous finding of a select committee of this House, it seems to me that there is little left for the members of this House to do but to express appreciation to the gentlemen who have worked so industriously, so carefully, and so thoughtfully in regard to this important subject, and to assure the Government that if the recommendations of the committee are carried out they will meet with the approval of every one.
One further thought occurs to me, speaking of industrial research in particular, and that is that this is a day when a great deal is being said about the importance of increased production. Men are too apt to think of production as being dependent wholly upon what economists used to

speak of as land, labour and capital, or natural resources, labour and capital, forgetting altogether the enormous significance, as regards production, of scientific research. And it is to emphasize what scientific research means, not in one direction only, but in all directions, that I am taking just a moment longer to refer to that point.
All of the work of labour is vastly enhanced and increased in its opportunity and in its rewards by the extent to which scientific research is applied to the problems of industry. The return to capital, and the possibility of greatly increased returns, is similarly enhanced; and so far as the community is concerned its well-being is also enhanced in the same way. I think in our discussion of commercial and industrial problems we are too much inclined to forget the work carried on in the libraries and laboratories by men who are little heard of in public, but who, after all, perhaps, more than any other class in society, are responsible for the progress of mankind. If the Government by establishing an institute of the kind suggested here can in this Dominion help to promote scientific research in ways which I hope will not only parallel and rival, but will in. some respects possibly outrun, what has been done in other countries, we shall not only contribute to our own industrial, social and commercial well-being, but we shall help, I believe in the advancement of other nations as well.
Let me say also that scientific reseach in industry is not only the handmaid of these different factors of production; it seems to me it is not less the handmaid, and the necessary handmaid, of governmental policies in such matters as transportation, commerce, immigration, colonization, or any other particular policy which relates to the commercial and industrial life of the country. Unless scientific research is applied in all of these particular branches, the outcome of any policy adopted by a government will never be what it should be in the development of the country's welfare.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I particularly welcome what this report seems to suggest in the way of closer cooperation between the universities of our country and governmental administration. I think that everything is to be gained by having the universities and the government brought into close touch with each other. University men should take as large a part as possible in the affairs of their country, in its government and in the administration

of its departments, and our governments should, I think, do as much as they reasonably can to encourage and make possible the work of our universities on a scale which is befitting the great opportunities confronting them-and as one hon. member said this evening, there is no doubt whatever that our .universities are not in a position to cope single-handed with the great needs of scientific research. In promoting scientific research, the Government must co-operate with the universities, and I was glad to hear my hon. friend from London emphasize as clearly as he did, and in that fine, eloquent and, if I may so describe it, imaginative way he has of expressing himself, that the universities would receive a greater assistance through an Industrial Research Institute of this kind than could be possible without such an undertaking.
I have great pleasure indeed as a member of this House in supporting most heartily the recommendations of the committee. It is gratifying to see that those recommendations are unanimous. I think we owe a word of thanks to all the members of the committee, and especially to the 'chairman who has given so much of his time and thought to the work of that committee.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What I have to say tonight will be exceedingly short.
And sweet.

I wish I could in the brevity of my remarks make them as pithy in one direction as I am sure the Chairman of the Committee would wish; but there are limitations of course which we find ourselves in contact with, and which, whether we wish it or not, restrain in many ways the practical embodiment of the sympathies and goodwill of the Government.
I have been particularly pleased with the tone of the debate-not speaking of tone in the usual way, but in regard to the line of intelligent appreciation and presentation of the subject itself. Not merely a sentimental support has been given, but a support of insight and of real connection between the mind and the heart of the speaker and the principles of the subject under discussion.
As one heard successive speakers talking of the marvellous things which had been done by science, and which we ourselves had forgotten in a good many respects until they were brought to our attention to-night, one wondered why people run into other channels for the wonders of romance. Really

the greatest romances, particularly of the last centuries, have been found in the development of scientific thought and in the scientific research earned on by the quiet workers of the world. They come upon us one after the other; the story passes, and then we are apt to forget. When we have a summing up, such as we have had to-night, we are impressed with the wonderful phases of the development of humanity which has taken place during the last fifty, sixty or one hundred years.
As to the matter which is directly before us, I will spare the blushes of the member for London (Mr. Cronyn) by not reiterating what has already been said by many of those who have spoken. But while sparing his blushes, I do not want him to think that I do not in my heart thank him for the work which he and his willing and efficient committee have performed in connection with this matter and for the way in which they have presented the subject to us to-night. We must not forget, either, that during the l^st five years, as was mentioned by the member for Calgary West (Mr. Tweedie) we have been doing a little towards maintaining and extending the interest in this matter through the Advisory Research Council. Things of this kind proceed step by step,- here a little, and there a little. Without a doubt we are working up to the point where we shall have in Canada some such efficient mechanism as has been described here to-night. I wish we could work it out now, but there are considerations which make that difficult. I am not, however, without hope that we may, even this year, -make a beginning in the direction of carrying out the report-something, at least, which will be an earnest of the completion of the project as soon as possible. In a way, it is a kind of irony that the very thing which has made it particularly necessary that an impetus should be given to scientific research and the alliance of scientific effort with industrial development, the war, has so crippled us that we cannot do what we would like to do in this respect. Science does two things: it puts within the power of the destructive elements of war vast enginery and machinery for completing the destruction upon which it is bent, and almost at the same time it stretches out the hand of solace, comfort, help to the victims of the destruction which it has thus helped to create. If the war has made wounds, deep and gaping, and broad, and if science has helped to make those wounds, science to-day is putting all its resources and its effort into the healing of those wounds, into the
bringing of a normal period and, subsequently, a more progressive period of development in all these matters, not leaving out that which is probably the greatest good that can come from the development of science,-the betterment of the world and the greater wellbeing of all those who live in it. For after all, science is to he judged, not by the material development which it first brings about, but by the extent to which it promotes the comfort, happiness and uplift of the people; by the general good which it accomplishes for the world.
I want to reiterate my thanks and the thanks of the Government for the good work which hals been done by the member for London and his committee, and to assure them that it will not be allowed to pass without fruit. I hope that something may be done alt an early day; that if all we would like - to do cannot be 'accomplished, at least a beginning may be made. I shall bring the matter to the- attention of my colleagues, and I know that I shall have a sympathetic set of colleagues, whether or not we 'shall be table to cross all the ditches and make all the progress we would like to make at this particular time.
